[p. 329] **Sūrat al-Furqān**

Its purpose is to warn all those who are accountable of His, glorified be He, comprehensive power, which entails complete knowledge, and which is indicated by this clear Qur'an. That entails that there is, in reality, no existent other than Him. So He is the Truth, and whatever is other than Him is false. Its being named *al-Furqān* (the Criterion) clearly indicates this, for the Book was sent down only to distinguish between what is ambiguous and to differentiate truth from falsehood, (﴿so that whoever perishes might perish by clear proof, and whoever lives might live by clear proof﴾ [al-Anfāl: 42]), so that no one will have a proof against Allah.

**In the name of Allah** (the One to whom belongs the conclusive proof, due to the all-encompassing scope of His greatness and the comprehensiveness of His knowledge and power), **the Most Gracious** (who, by His blessings, has encompassed the Criterion, for the people of faith and of disbelief alike), **the Most Merciful** (who singles out whomever He wills of His servants with the garments of good pleasure).

When He, glorified be He, concluded the previous surah with the vastness of dominion, the comprehensiveness of knowledge, the exaltation of the Messenger, [p. 330] and the threat to whoever transgresses the limit, He opened this one with the like of that, in a manner that—although it is grander than that—is a proof of it. So He said, **﴿Blessed is He﴾**, meaning: He is established in a state of stability accompanied by the blessing and goodness through which mercy has preceded wrath, and in His exaltedness in attributes and acts, so that no stability can approach His. This is not so except through the perfection of His power, and His power is not perfected except through the comprehensiveness of His knowledge. This verb is the intransitive form (*muṭāwiʿ*) of *bāraka*, and it is specific to Allah, Exalted is He; it has not been used for anyone else. For this reason it is not inflected for the future tense or as an active participle. Then He described His noble Self with what indicates this, saying: **﴿Who﴾**.

Since repeating the warning—which is the aim of the surah—is more beneficial, and distributing it over successive times is more effective in shaking hearts and restraining them, and since clarifying difficulties in distinguishing between what is ambiguous is more helpful for what would otherwise be a cause (of error), He expressed it with what indicates distinction and placed it first, saying: **﴿has sent down the Criterion﴾**, meaning: the Book which was sent down to the worldly heaven and was then a book; then it was sent down in installments according to what is beneficial. For this reason it was named *al-Furqān*. It is also because it is the distinguisher between what is ambiguous, so it leaves no obscurity unless it clarifies it, no true matter unless it establishes it, and no falsehood unless it negates and annihilates it. In it is the ordering of the first life [p. 331] and the next. Thus it is a decisive proof of the knowledge of the One who sent it down. And from His overwhelming knowledge is His sending it down **﴿upon His servant﴾**, meaning the one who has no greater right to be attributed to His noble pronoun, because he is sincerely His, with no admixture of anyone else in him at all. No created being has attained what he attained of the purity of dispositions and the loftiness of aspirations. There is no doubt that the Messenger indicates his Sender to the extent of His knowledge, the multitude of His hosts, and the breadth of His dominion: **﴿Allah knows best where to place His message﴾** [al-Anʿām: 124]. Then He gave the reason for sending it down upon him by His saying: **﴿that it may be a warner﴾**, meaning the servant or the Criterion.

Since the "worlds" (*ʿālamīn*) are everything other than Allah, and since someone might claim that what is meant is only a part, because the word is sometimes applied to a part of its meaning by way of inclusion (*dalālat al-taḍammun*), and since the plural must necessarily convey what the singular conveys with an addition, He used the plural to make known that what is meant is the direct denotation (*al-madlūl al-muṭābaqī*), together with an explicit statement of the encompassing of all the categories that fall under the concept of the singular. He chose the plural form for rational beings by way of predominance (*taghlīb*), to inform that they are the primary intended ones. So He said: **﴿to the worlds﴾**, meaning all accountable beings: the jinn, the humans, and the angels.

Since each of the Book and the one to whom it was sent down is profound in its meaning, He expressed it with what may be intended to mean the one warned and the warning, in an emphatic manner, saying: **﴿a warner﴾**, meaning: and a bringer of glad tidings. He restricted it to warning only to allude to glad tidings through the word **"Blessed"** (*tabāraka*), and because the context calls for it, since He concluded the previous surah with the turning away of those who turn their backs on the rulings, [p. 332] and the negation of faith from them through the negation of submission. In this there is an allusion to the multitude of those deserving of warning. There is no heed to whoever says that al-Rāzī and al-Nasafī (al-Burhān al-Nasafī) transmitted a consensus (*ijmāʿ*, scholarly agreement) that the Prophet ﷺ was not sent to the angels. For al-Rāzī's wording in some copies of his tafsir is: "*Lakunnā ajmaʿnā ʿalā annahu lam yursal ilā al-malāʾika*" (but we are agreed that he was not sent to the angels), while in most copies it reads: "*bayyannā*" (we have made clear) instead of "*ajmaʿnā*" (we are agreed). Even if all copies agreed on it, it would not harm, because it is not explicit in intending a consensus. Also, consensus is not established by a single transmission, especially in a matter where the indications cohere against it, and no preventing evidence has come concerning it. As for al-Nasafī, he took from al-Rāzī and expressed it in his wording, so the two became one. I have explained this at His, exalted is He, saying in Sūrat al-Anʿām:

**﴿that I may warn you thereby, and whoever it reaches﴾** [al-Anʿām: 19], with a satisfying explanation that leaves no doubt. Indeed, even if it were said that the verse is upon its apparent meaning, with no specificity to rational beings, and that each thing is addressed according to its nature, it would be a valid view. Imam Tāj al-Dīn al-Subkī expressly stated this at the beginning of *al-Tarshīḥ*, in his saying: "And I invoke blessings upon His Prophet Muḥammad, the chosen one, sent to every thing." Likewise al-Muḥibb al-Ṭabarī at the end of *al-Qurā li-qāṣidī Umm al-Qurā*. That is because the Prophet ﷺ never called upon anything inanimate or moving other than a human except that it responded to him with what is required by **﴿We offered the trust to the heavens and the earth and the mountains, but they refused to bear it﴾** [al-Aḥzāb: 72]. He called several branches of trees more than once, and they came to him prostrating; then he commanded them to return to their places, and they did. He called the lizard (*ḍabb*) and other dumb animals, and they obeyed him. He called the trees more than once, and they heard and came hastening to him. He commanded the mountain when it trembled, and it submitted. He sent to palm trees and stones, commanding them to gather so that he might fulfil a need with them, and they did; then he sent commanding them to return to their places, and they answered. He struck the ground and water gushed forth from it. He sent his arrow into the well and it bubbled up with abundant water. And other things, which are contained in the proofs of prophethood. Indeed, he never called an infant at the breast except that it bore witness to him, because it is upon the primordial nature (*fiṭra*). All of this indicates the apparent meaning of the verse, which requires an increase in his honour ﷺ, without any objectionable consequence arising from it and without any text contradicting it. And Allah is the Guide.

Abū Jaʿfar Ibn al-Zubayr said in his *Burhān*: Since Sūrat al-[p. 333]-Nūr contained the explanation of many rulings, such as the ruling on fornication, the accusation of wives with it, slander, seeking permission (to enter), the veil, aiding the poor, the contract of manumission (*kitāba*), and other things; and the disclosure of hidden matters, of varying states, by knowing which and being informed of which the wicked is distinguished from the good—such as His, glorified be He, informing His Prophet and the believers of what the people of the slander had fabricated, and the explanation of their evil condition and the collapse of their schemes, in the story of the hypocrites, in their showing the opposite of what they conceal; then His generous promise to the rightly-guided caliphs: **﴿Allah has promised those of you who believe﴾** [al-Nūr: 55]; then what He exposed of the hypocrites of the Trench: **﴿Allah already knows those among you who slip away covertly﴾** [al-Nūr: 63], to the end of the verse—all of this was a criterion by which faith is strengthened, and which no one who acknowledges the Most Gracious denies, testifying to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ for the soundness of his message, and clarifying the import of His saying **﴿Do not make the calling of the Messenger among you like the calling of one another﴾** [al-Nūr: 63], from the great rank of his ﷺ and his high majesty. Allah, glorified be He, followed it with His saying: **﴿Blessed is He who has sent down the Criterion upon His servant﴾**, which is the Qur'an that distinguishes between truth and falsehood, and that informs about what the hypocrites concealed and hid of deception and disbelief, **﴿that he may be a warner to the worlds﴾**, so that he may warn them against the misdeeds of the hypocrites and against imitating them. Then the speech was woven together [p. 334] and the sublime pattern of that order was joined. This surah contained a censure of the disbelievers and a description of their slander and the evil of their deeds, to a degree not contained in many of its counterparts, such as their saying:

**﴿What is this messenger that eats food?﴾** [al-Furqān: 7], and the verses that follow it; their saying **﴿Why have not angels been sent down to us, or why do we not see our Lord?﴾** [al-Furqān: 21]; their saying **﴿Why was the Qur'an not sent down to him all at once?﴾** [al-Furqān: 32]; and their saying **﴿And what is the Most Gracious?﴾** [al-Furqān: 60]; and what supports these and runs through them. For this reason the surah was concluded with the decisive threat and the most severe warning, which is His, glorified be He, saying: **﴿So you have denied; so the punishment will be inevitable﴾** [al-Furqān: 77]. End.

The Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 25, verse 2:

When the mention of the One who sent down the Criterion (al-Furqan), glorified is He, and the mention of the Criterion and of the One upon whom it was sent down, had been made in summary form, He followed this with its detailed explanation in order. He began by describing the Sender, glorified is He, with that which is the clearest proof of the intent to generalize the message to everyone who wills it. So He said: ﴿The One to whom belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾, that is, alone, ﴿the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾; therefore there is no denial that He should send a messenger to all who are in them. ﴿And He has not taken a son﴾, so that He would be haughty toward His messenger. ﴿And there is not for Him a partner in dominion﴾, so that he could oppose Him in the message or share it with Him, whereby some of the creation would be outside His message, or would be observing a command other than His command.

Since the standing of a thing at a limit, such that it cannot go beyond it to the limit of some other thing, is evident, this is an animal that cannot make itself an inanimate object (p-336), nor [something] higher than the animal; and this is an inanimate object that cannot make itself an animal, nor lower than the rank of the inanimate object; and so on, to other things that the creation is unable to explain, indicating that it is created and nurtured. He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And He created every thing﴾, that is, brought it into being with measure and proportion, ﴿every thing﴾, that is, of what they claimed had a son or a partner or other than that.

Since He had proportioned every thing to what suits it and prepared it for that, He said, explaining and verifying the meaning of "created": ﴿And He determined it﴾ in its origination without disparity, ﴿with determination﴾, that is, that thing cannot exceed what it was created for, prepared for and made easy for, to something else, in any way whatsoever.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 25, verse 3:

When he had reminded them of the knowledge that He had fixed in their natures (fitrah), he marvelled at them, for every person of intellect, in a circumstantial clause, at their opposing what they witnessed for themselves. So he said, with the agent (fa'il) left implicit, as an indication of the reprehensibility of attributing this act to a specific agent, both as a rebuke to them and as a guidance toward every listener's immediately rejecting that attribution from Him: ﴿And they have taken﴾, that is, the worshippers of idols imposed upon themselves to be taken.

Since His exaltedness cannot be limited, and the lower ranks cannot be counted, he drew attention to this with the preposition, saying: ﴿besides Him﴾, that is, after the proof had been established that He alone is the God, from the aspects that were previously mentioned, ﴿gods﴾, which are unified and visible, because, as God Most High said: ﴿they create nothing﴾, that is, there is no greater incapacity than theirs: from them there can be no bringing into existence of anything, in contrast to those who worship them.

Since the contentious objector might claim that, despite this, they are not created, he said: ﴿while they are created﴾, that is, as witnessed in them by change and by their submission to His will, glorified is He; and among that is that their worshippers fashioned them by carving and sculpting.

When he had established that He had blessed everything, and blessings are more numerous in existence, and the least blessing upon a thing is His creating it, he informed that those others cannot have power over their own harm or over their annihilation. So he said, expressing with the particle used for rational beings, in mockery of their worshippers in placing them in that station, or by way of giving precedence to the rational, since they worshipped the angels, Uzair and the Messiah, peace be upon them: ﴿and they have no power﴾, that is, it does not occur to them in any way that they could possess ﴿for themselves any harm﴾; for this reason he put it first, and made it indefinite so that it would be general.

Thus, when it was established by this that they are His creation, but the contentious objector might say, "They have power over that, but they deliberately leave it," because no one wants harm to himself, he said: ﴿nor benefit﴾, that is, not even by remaining in one state; and their worshippers are able, by way of acquisition (kasb), to do what God wills of that, so they are higher than them, and the worship of the higher by one beneath it is not among the acts of rational people.

When death and life are of such great importance that nothing else is comparable to them, he repeated the operator, saying: ﴿and they have no power﴾, and he put death first because life is greater. So he said, beginning with what belongs to the category of harm, in the same sequence as what came before: ﴿over death﴾, that is, neither for themselves nor for others, ﴿nor life﴾, that is, from non-existence, ﴿nor resurrection﴾, that is, the restoring of what was folded up of life by death. He joined them with the conjunction "wa" (and), although some of them are a consequence of what precedes, to indicate that each one of them is sufficient to negate divinity from them, given the established incapacity.

When he had described the One who sent down the Criterion (al-Furqan) with attributes that no one other than Him knows in full, and the miraculousness of the revealed text that makes this clear, namely this Qur'an, and that it alone is the Criterion, he expressed wonder at the state of those who denied it. He said, in place of "and they said," ﴿And those who disbelieved said﴾, making apparent the quality that led them to this statement, which is concealing what was manifest to them and to others, like the sun, and striving to hide it: ﴿This is not﴾, that is, the Qur'an is not, ﴿except a falsehood﴾, that is, a lie turned away from its apparent and proper meaning, which is the worst of lies, ﴿that he has fabricated﴾, that is, deliberately invented this lie, this warner (al-Nadhir). Thus their saying was a matter for wonder, because its defect is evident.

Since a human being is naturally inclined to take pride in even the slightest of virtues, loving that they be attributed to him and that none of them be ascribed to another, their saying was even more wondrous and more manifestly defective: ﴿And others helped him﴾, that is, Muhammad, ﴿in it﴾, that is, in the Qur'an, ﴿a people﴾, that is, men of means who had been given what distinguishes them above others. They added to their distance by saying ﴿others﴾, that is, from outside his own people. It was said that they meant the Jews, and it was said that they meant others in his land among the slaves, Christians and others. Therefore the words of the Exalted were a consequence of this: ﴿Then they have brought﴾, that is, the disbelievers in this matter, ﴿injustice﴾, by placing falsehood on what is neither more truthful nor more just, ﴿and falsehood (zur)﴾, that is, a deviation together with great coarseness from the straight path, in attributing to the most truthful of people and the purest of them in character and the most upright of them in conduct these base things, which the basest of people would not accept for himself. For these, even though they are vile in themselves, are certain to bring disgrace. Ibn Jarir said: the root of zur is making falsehood appear good and distorting speech.

Now, when his contradiction had been made clear: first, in their claim that the Qur'an contains what is plainly incompatible with its description; and second, that he was helped in it after the form *ifti'al* (reflexive verb pattern, here indicating effort or self-directed action) had indicated solitary composition, He, exalted is He, followed it with another contradiction on their part, saying in an expression of wonder: ﴿And they said﴾ (p-340), that is, the disbelievers, ﴿"Fables of the ancients"﴾, the plural of *isṭāra* and *usṭūra* (fable, legend), such as the tales of Rustam and Isfandiyar. Thus they declared that he had no part in it. ﴿"He has had them written down"﴾, that is, he sought to have them copied for himself. ﴿"So they are dictated"﴾, that is, as a consequence of his effort, they are ﴿dictated﴾ (*tumlā*), meaning recited, by one who dictates them, skillfully, renewed and continuous, ﴿"to him"﴾ from the book in which he had them written, during his free times, ﴿"morning and evening"﴾, before people disperse, ﴿"and evening"﴾, that is, in the afternoon, when they return to their dwellings. Or, it means constantly, so that he would labor to memorize them after having labored to acquire them through copying, which shows that he is unlettered. And this, as you see, is not said by anyone who has any sense in his mind or any dignity, for it is among the known matters that are not hidden from any intelligent person that if a man were to keep company with something for ten days, morning and evening, there would not remain anyone among those who know him and are aware of his circumstances who would not know that about him. So if he were to deny it afterward, he would be disgraced with a disgrace whose stain would never be washed away. How much more so when the town is small, and the man is great and famous? They claimed that he persisted in this until the time of their statement and afterward continues without ceasing. They reproached him for being poor, needing to walk in the markets, while he calls them to contest him, even with a single surah like it, and among them are the scribes, the poets (p-341), the eloquent, and the orators, and he has more wealth than them and greater helpers, yet they are not able to do so.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 25, verse 6:

When they had accused him of these statements, in which they are floundering in blind confusion, and although these statements are clearly defective to anyone with even slight insight, they did gain some currency among some of the Arabs, given the breadth of their intellects and the soundness of their thinking, owing to flimsy doubts in which imitation (taqlid) had established them, and the strong attachment to what they had been upon for a long time, He (glorified is He) commanded him to answer them, resuming, and He said: ﴿Say﴾, i.e., indicating the falsity of what they had said and threatening them: ﴿He sent it down﴾, i.e., the Qur'an, from the treasuries of His knowledge, contrary to everything you have fabricated, ﴿who knows the secret﴾, i.e., all of it, nothing of it is hidden from Him, so how much more the open! ﴿in the heavens and the earth﴾. So He will answer you concerning everything you have fabricated against Me and against His Book, even if you conceal it, and He will explain everything that the servants need in both abodes, in a speech that is miraculous in wording and meaning, in a manner by which every person of understanding will verify that it could only be said by one who knows all knowables, and none other than Him encompasses all knowables. This is very evident from His informing about the past in a way that the scholars of earlier times confirm, and His judgment about the future in a way that is an unfailing decisive stroke, and His bringing forth the hidden and making firm all that He says. Moreover, it has been the custom of Him (glorified and exalted is He) to take vengeance on whoever lies about Him: first by exposing his lie, then by seizing him, and thirdly by punishing him with the greatest punishment. So you will see who does that to him, and by my life, his truthfulness has already become clear through the occurrence of the three matters.

Since it is known that the One who knows everything is capable of everything, as its affirmation has passed in Surat Ta-Ha, and it has been the custom that whoever knows that another mocks him and is able to act against him hastens to seize him, an answer is given to one who as if said: "Why does He not destroy those who deny Him?" by His saying, encouraging them to repentance, pointing to His power through concealment and bounty, and explaining the benefit of sending down this Reminder to them, namely returning from what they had persisted in for their long ages of disbelief and various sins: ﴿Indeed He is always﴾, without beginning and without end, ﴿Forgiving﴾, i.e., most thorough in concealing whatever sins of His servants He wills, by not reproaching them for them nor taking them to account for them, ﴿Merciful﴾ toward them in bestowing favors upon them after creating them, through providing for them, placing intellects within them, establishing proofs for them, sending messengers and sending down books to them, and granting them respite in their denial. That is, there is no cause for their respite and admonition by what He has sent down to them except His mercy, His forgiveness, and His knowledge that His Book is a source of rectitude for their conditions in both abodes.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 25, verse 7:

When He, glorified is He, had completed what He willed of mentioning the abode and the one who dwells in it, and had informed of their criticism concerning the abode, which is the principal object of the message, and had established that proof against their falsehood, He followed it with an account of their criticism of the Messenger who brought it. He addressed, in wonder, their minds, which they consider the purest of minds in thought and the highest in effects, regarding what they displayed of that, which they supposed to be evidence against the message, while none of it is fit to be a doubt for anyone possessing even a grain of sense in such a matter, let alone to be evidence. ﴿And they said﴾, i.e., asking in mockery of his description and disparaging him through his conduct, the speech of one who is certain that the attribute of the message contradicts him: ﴿What is this﴾. The pointing in this manner conveys contempt and belittlement. Then they displayed their derision by saying: ﴿messenger﴾, i.e., the one who claims that he has been singled out from the rest of mankind in this age by this lofty attribute, ﴿who eats food﴾, i.e., just as we eat, ﴿and walks in the markets﴾, i.e., which are the places of worldly pursuits, just as we walk.

Since the sense of what came before was: "What does he have that is like us, while he claims exclusivity over us in the message?", they followed it with reproach for his not being accompanied by any of the forms of distinction, by way of supposition, as an answer to one who seems to have said: "Then what should he do?" By their saying: ﴿Why has not﴾, i.e., "would that", and it comes for rebuke, and this is what they intend, ﴿an angel been sent down﴾, i.e., from heaven, from whatever abode it may be, arriving ﴿to him﴾, i.e., in the form in which he is in heaven, ﴿an angel﴾, i.e., one of God's angels in their forms, which differ from the forms of the children of Adam, ﴿so that he might be﴾ (in the accusative, as an answer to the exhortation) that angel, even if he were a human, ﴿with him a warner﴾. Thus he would be distinguished by a state that none of us has, so that he would be more awe-inspiring in warning, because of the awe and strength he possesses. It seems they expressed it in the past tense to indicate that what they meant was his being, in their view, in a form other than the one in which he informs you of the continual descent of the angel upon him at every moment, concealed such that no one else sees him; or because the angel may be in a state of companionship with him for the purpose of warning, and it is only that he does not change from it by ascending to heaven or otherwise, unlike a treasure, which is for expenditure, so if it is not continually replenished it runs out. This is the secret of the use of ﴿to﴾ rather than ﴿upon﴾, which is for enveloping with revelation. For this reason they used the present tense in their saying, descending from the height of that rank:

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 25, verse 8:

﴿Aw yulqā﴾ (or a treasure be thrown down to him), i.e., from any thrower whatsoever.

Since throwing down (al-ilqā') indicates height, they departed from the particle of elevation used in Surah Hud, where the expression was "from" (al-inzāl), to the particle of ending (ḥarf al-nihāya), and said: ﴿ilayhi﴾ (to him). That is, if he does not have that state, ﴿kanz﴾ (a treasure), i.e., this matter is found in him and its throwing down to him is renewed, without his being concerned or regarding it, by raising him above our being common in every respect. Also, the expression in this and what follows in the present tense is more indicative of their eagerness for this world and that it is their greatest concern. Then they also descended (tanazzalū) in their saying: ﴿Aw takūnu lahu﴾ (or he has), i.e., if he has nothing of what has passed, ﴿jannatun﴾ (a garden), i.e., an orchard or a plantation, as some of our notables have, ﴿ya'kulu minhā﴾ (from which he eats), so that it frees him from what he occupies himself with at times, such as seeking a livelihood, and his wealth would be more honourable for him, more attracting of hearts towards him, more conducive to the gathering of followers around him, and more effective in what he wants. This is according to the reading of the majority with the yā' (third person), while according to the reading of Ḥamza and al-Kisā'ī with the nūn, the meaning is: if we are given power over it, that would be more attracting of us to following him. All of what they said is corrupt, since neither he (ﷺ) nor any of his followers claimed that he or any of the prophets before him was set apart from humankind, nor that any of the essential attributes of humans contradicts prophethood and messengership. As for accumulating worldly things, it is in most cases an obstacle to travelling to the abode of honour and the place of safety, and a bearer towards arrogance, and only the lowly of aspiration rejoice in it. And slight means in hand harms only a deficient person who asks people, explicitly or allusively, desiring to complete his deficiency with perishing trash; and God has honoured His Prophet (ﷺ) above that by what he has of the attributes of perfection and lofty morals.

When they, by this, were placing speech in other than its proper places, far from the way of correctness, He said, marvelling at their condition: ﴿Wa qāla al-ẓālimūn﴾ (And the wrongdoers said), and so He stated the description that made them so: ﴿in﴾ (not), i.e., you do not follow ﴿illā rajulan masḥūrā﴾ (except a man bewitched), i.e., one who speaks with what does not benefit him, so his condition in that regard is the condition of one whose intellect has been overcome by sorcery, or a sorcerer whose sorcery has become his nature, so that he separates by what he brings between a man and his wife, his child, and the like. They expressed it with the passive form to indicate this: that because of how often such things happen from him, it has become as though it arises from him against his will.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 25, verse 9:

When He, glorified be He, had completed what He mentioned of their statements arising from their misguidance, He, glorified be He, turned to His Messenger (ﷺ), consoling him, and said: ﴿Look﴾. Then He indicated their amazement at them, that what they said deserves to be questioned, by His saying: ﴿how they have coined for you the comparisons﴾, and He placed first that which is of concern, so He said: ﴿for you﴾. They made you, at one time, like them in need of food; at another time, their equal in seeking to reach gains and benefits through subtle cunning and sound intellect; at another time, one whose intellect is overcome and whose temperament is deranged, bringing what no sane person would accept; and at another time, a sorcerer, bringing what their powers cannot match and what baffles their thoughts. ﴿So they have strayed﴾, that is, from all the paths of justice and all the modes of clear reasoning, because of that, so they did not find a statement on which to settle, and they went very far astray. ﴿So they are not able﴾ at present nor in the outcome, because of this misguidance, ﴿to find a way﴾, that is, to follow a path among the paths that lead to what deserves to be sought. Rather, they are in desolate wildernesses and deadly deserts.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 25, verse 10:

Once it was established that they have no existence, because they have neither knowledge nor power, and that there is no blessing or goodness in them, neither for themselves nor for others, He (glorified is He) affirmed for Himself what befits Him of perfection, the perfection from which He bestows upon whomever He wills of His servants whatever He wills. So He said: ﴿Blessed is He﴾, meaning He is established in a permanence accompanied by goodness and blessing. There is no permanence except His, ﴿who, if He wills﴾, for none can compel Him, ﴿will give you better than that﴾, that is, than what they said in mockery. Then He replaced that with His words: ﴿gardens﴾, far more than a single garden, ﴿beneath which rivers flow﴾, meaning its land will be springs gushing forth, that is, every place where a river is intended to flow will have one flowing. So it will always be irrigated, enriching its owner from every need, and he will not need to water it in cultivating it.

Since the palace (qasr), which is the house of the lofty building, is not something in which the giving is continuous, like the garden whose description this is, He expressed it in the present tense, signalling renewal whenever a flaw occurs that would impair the reality of the palace. So He said: ﴿and will give you palaces﴾, meaning lofty houses in which you dwell with what befits them of attendants and servants. Al-Baghawi said: the Arabs call every lofty house a qasr.

This phrase is suitable for Him (glorified is He) to grant that in this world, as a thing that would crush their resolve and, fearing its consequences, would have eased their submission, because they knew that the one who sent him is able to do whatever He wills. However, He (glorified is He) made him independent of that through His support with helpers, from among the angels, mankind and jinn, until their affair was ruined and their patience worn thin. And He did not will what this noble verse indicates in this fleeting world, but deferred it to the enduring Hereafter. He (glorified is He) had offered him what he wished of that in this world, and he refused it. Al-Baghawi narrated through the route of Ibn al-Mubarak, and al-Tirmidhi, who said it is hasan, from Abu Umamah (may Allah be pleased with him), from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "My Lord offered me that He would make the plain of Makkah gold for me. I said: 'No, my Lord! Rather, I would be satisfied one day and hungry one day. When I am hungry, I will humble myself to You and call upon You, and when I am satisfied, I will praise You and thank You.'"

It is also narrated through the route of Abu al-Shaykh, from 'A'ishah (may Allah be pleased with her), who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Had I wished, mountains of gold would have travelled with me. An angel came to me, whose loincloth was worth the Ka'bah, and said: 'Your Lord sends you His greetings and says to you: If you wish, be a prophet-servant; and if you wish, be a prophet-king.' I looked at Jibril (peace be upon him), and he gestured to me: 'Humble yourself.' So I said: 'A prophet-servant.'" She said: After that, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would not eat reclining and would say: "I eat as a servant eats, and I sit as a servant sits."

What completes this will come in surah Saba' at His words ﴿and We caused a spring of molten copper to flow for him﴾ [Saba': 12]. And it is not far from my mind that the noble verse, although in the form of a conditional, points to what Allah opened for him (ﷺ) of gardens, the like of which were not in the lands of the Arabs, when Allah opened Khaybar and Wadi al-Qura to him, and he disposed of them personally and ate from them; and it points to what He opened to his Companions after him of the lands of Persia and Rome, with their palaces and gardens, for which there is no equal. For this reason He expressed the gardens in the past tense and the palaces in the present tense, and they were given the treasures of Kisra ibn Hurmuz. For what befits the station of kings is that their indications be broader than their expressions. When they mention something possible by way of supposition, it is among their intentions to bring it into being. They love to be satisfied with a mere gesture from them, and that their hint be relied upon more than others' explicit statements, and that what they suppose be treated as what is firmly affirmed by others, and that what is possible in their speech be treated as what is obligatory. So what is your opinion of the King of kings, who is able to do everything? He (glorified is He) has directed the address to the people of the highest understanding and the greatest knowledge, and He showed him (glorified is He) what would come about from that after him, at the Battle of the Trench.

Al-Bayhaqi narrated in Dala'il al-Nubuwwah, from 'Amr ibn 'Awf al-Muzani (may Allah be pleased with him) that when the Prophet (ﷺ) marked out the Trench for digging, he assigned forty cubits for every ten men. Salman al-Farisi (may Allah be pleased with him) was a strong man, and the Muhajirun and the Ansar disputed over him, so the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Salman is one of us, the People of the House." Then a white, rounded rock appeared to them. 'Amr said: It broke our iron tools and was hard on us. So we said: "O Salman, go up to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and inform him of the news of this rock." He informed him, and the Prophet (ﷺ) took the pickaxe from Salman and struck it three blows, cracking it with each blow, and shattering it on the third. With each blow a flash appeared that lit up what lay between the two lava plains of Madinah, until it was as if a lamp were in the middle of a dark house. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said Allahu akbar with each flash. Then he took Salman's hand and climbed up. Salman asked him, and he said to the people: "Did you see what Salman said?" They said: "Yes, O Messenger of Allah! May our fathers and mothers be your ransom! We saw you strike and a flash came out like a wave, and we saw you say Allahu akbar; we saw nothing else." He said: "In the first flash the palaces of al-Hirah and the cities of Kisra were illuminated for me, as if they were the fangs of dogs. And from the second, the red palaces of the land of Rome, as if they were the fangs of dogs. And from the third, the palaces of San'a', as if they were the fangs of dogs. And Jibril (peace be upon him) informed me that my nation will prevail over them."

The Muslims rejoiced and said: "Praise be to Allah! A true promise: He promised us victory after siege." Then the confederates appeared, and the Muslims said: "This is what Allah and His Messenger promised us, and it increased them only in faith and submission" [al-Ahzab: 22].

The hypocrites said about that what Allah the Exalted indicated in the Qur'an. Then Allah the Exalted disproved the hypocrites and confirmed His Messenger (ﷺ). His Companions (may Allah be pleased with them all) opened all that he mentioned, and they prevailed over the whole realm of Persia, Yemen and most of Rome, and they seized from the treasures of Kisra and Caesar what cannot be counted. The Prophet (ﷺ) had disposed of that from that time as kings dispose of their wealth, for Allah's promise has no breaking of it; rather, what is absent of it is greater than what is present of others, and what is promised to him is more certain than what is immediately at hand from anything else. So he (ﷺ) gave Tamim ibn Aws al-Dari the land of the Khalil (peace be upon him), from the land of al-Sham, from the realm of Rome. And he gave Kharim ibn Aws, who is called Shuwayl, the honour of Karamah, daughter of 'Abd al-Masih ibn Baqilah, from the captives of al-Hirah, from the lands of Iraq, from the realm of Persia. Each of them took possession of what was given to him at the conquest, as one who has studied the books of conquests knows, during the days of the Rightly Guided Caliphs (may Allah be pleased with them all). So in my view this is among what the noble verse indicated: Allah the Exalted cleared His Prophet (ﷺ) of it and opened it for his Companions, as an honour to them by removing the people of polytheism from it, a favour upon them through it, a confirmation of His promise, and an honour to His Prophet (ﷺ) by the victory of his friends and the multiplication of his nation. Many of those who had said ﴿What is this Messenger that...﴾ [al-Furqan: 7] to the end of the verse were present at that. He had been able to strengthen him with all of that before his death, but He did not do so, because that would have been more evident in the matter, for his victory was contrary to how the people of this world are victorious, without many visible armies, nor abundant wealth, nor powerful helping kings. Rather, the kings were against him, and then they all became the most insignificant thing to him, at the hands of his Companions after him and his beloved ones.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 25, verse 11:

When it was established, by what He affirmed of His own noble perfection, that nothing prevents the bringing into being of what they proposed in a reproachful manner except the absence of will, not an incapacity on the part of the Creator nor a lowliness in the one for whom it is created, as consolation to him (ﷺ) in a style that indicates that He will give him that, He also consoled him by [showing] that they do not believe in the reality of what they attributed to him. So He turned away from their speech, saying: ﴿Rather﴾, meaning: do not think that they denied what you brought because they believe in you to be a liar and a fabricator of the Qur'an, or [believe there is] a deficiency in your eating food and walking in the markets, or in some aspect of your circumstances. Or [it means]: do not think that they deny His, the Exalted's, power to do what He mentioned, that if He willed He could make it for you. Or the meaning is: leave off reflecting on what they said about this, for they did not confine their denial to him, but ﴿they denied the Hour﴾, meaning, His power over it. That settled in their souls for long ages, and they took it over from predecessor to successor, and the love of this perishing trash was infused into their hearts, and their imaginations were bound to these outward appearances like beasts. So it was difficult for them to be disentangled from that by the clear proof that came to them, which they could not doubt, and so they became bold in obstinacy for this reason, through lack of fear of the terrors of the Day of Resurrection, as the Exalted said concerning the People of the Book:

﴿And what they used to invent deceived them in their religion﴾ [Al-Imran: 24]

﴿And We have prepared﴾, meaning: and the state is that We have prepared, that is, made ready, by what We possess of greatness, ﴿for whoever denies﴾ of these and others ﴿the Hour a blazing Fire﴾, meaning: a fire of intense blazing, by which they magnified the burning in the hearts of those who denied the prophets, peace be upon them, and their followers, may Allah be pleased with them.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 25, verse 12:

﴿When it sees them﴾ meaning: when it is in such a position that it is possible for them to see it, and for it to see them if it had sight, ﴿from a far place﴾, which is the farthest distance from which it is possible to see it, while they are being driven toward it. ﴿They will hear for it﴾, meaning specifically, ﴿a raging﴾, meaning a sound of its boiling and seething, like the sound of one enraged in his fury and agitation when his chest surges with anger, ﴿and a roaring﴾, meaning a sound that indicates the utmost extent of wrath. Its root meaning is a sound heard from the innermost part of the body (al-jawf).

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 25, verse 13:

When he had described their encounter with it (the Fire), he described their being cast into it. He said: ﴿And when they are thrown into it﴾, meaning they are cast down with humiliation, so that they are made to meet with it in the most degrading manner, ﴿into a narrow place therein﴾, meaning in the Fire, ﴿a place﴾. He described it with His words ﴿narrow﴾, adding to its dreadfulness, ﴿bound together﴾ in the most degrading manner, their hands bound to their necks in chains, or in ropes of palm fiber (masad), or together with the devils who led them astray. The taqrin (binding together) is the joining of one thing to another with a qirn, which is a rope. ﴿There they will cry out for destruction﴾, meaning in that hateful place, far removed from kindness, ﴿destruction﴾, meaning great ruin. So they say: "Woe to us!" because they have no companion other than it, and no one present with them besides it. Ibn Jarir said: The root of tabr (destruction) in the speech of the Arabs is turning away from something. The meaning then is: they call for their turning away from Paradise to the Fire, which they caused by their turning away from faith to disbelief. So they have no companion except their summoning of this, out of regret and remorse. Then they are answered, by way of resumption, with His words, exalted is He.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 25, verse 14:

﴿Do not call out for one destruction today⁠—﴾ O disbelievers, ﴿one destruction﴾, because you will not die when the causes of ruin descend upon you, ﴿but call out for many destructions﴾ which no counting can confine and which have no end, for you have fallen into that which necessitates it, since the kinds of ruin will never leave you at all, but there is no death.

Since the custom of the Arabs was to deem possible anything of creation that they feared, the situation called for asking them: Have they prepared a provision against what they were threatened with from the Creator, or not? This is in the context of asking about the comparison between it and what the God-fearing were promised, as an alert that it is of a higher rank than the merely possible, since it is certain to occur, and as a mockery of them. So He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Say: Is that better?﴾ meaning: this matter, terrifying in its dread, with which you were threatened, of the described Blaze (al-sa'ir).

Since it was the custom of the Arabs, in expressing the superiority of one thing over another, to use the form *af'al* (the elative, as in *khayr*, "better"), as an alert that the withholding of good from its opposite is hidden from no one, or that this is by way of concession and giving rein (*irkha' al-'inan*), as an alert to the intelligent person that it suffices him, in turning back from error, that there is a likelihood that what he is upon is inferior, He said: ﴿Or the Garden of Eternity?﴾ meaning: the abode that endures, ﴿which the God-fearing were promised﴾, meaning: the true and certain promise of it has come to pass, from the One whose promise is the promise, to those who feared and so believed in the Hour, placing between themselves and its terrors a protection from what the Messengers had commanded them. Then He, exalted is He, confirmed its matter as an emphasis on the glad tidings, by saying: ﴿It has been﴾, meaning: it came into being and was brought into existence by His creating, glorified is He, ﴿for them a reward﴾ for their belief and their deeds, ﴿and a destination﴾, meaning: a settled abode and an end. This is praise of their reward, for when it is in a spacious, pleasant place, it is more wholesome and sweeter for them, just as punishment, when it is in a narrow, dreadful place, is more painful and more agonizing. This is an interrogation of rebuke and reproach toward whoever has intellect and yet deems the possible things likely.

[p-357] When He, may He be exalted, mentioned their bliss in it, He mentioned their enjoyment within it, saying: ﴿For them therein﴾, that is, in the Garden specifically and not in anything else, ﴿whatever they wish﴾ of everything their souls desire, ﴿abiding eternally﴾, not seeking any change from it. ﴿It was﴾, that is, all of that, ﴿upon your Lord﴾, that is, the One who bestows favour upon you by bestowing kindness upon your followers, ﴿a promise﴾.

When He, glorified is He, indicated that this was obligatory upon His own great self, by the expression "upon" and by the promise, and since man, especially being disposed to dignity of self, hardly consents to ask for what he does not expect to obtain, He said: ﴿to be asked for﴾, that is, deserving to be asked for its fulfilment, because one who asks is worthy of having his request answered and his hopes and expectations realised. The meaning is that when the asking of the one promised is joined to His making the matter binding upon Himself, [p-357 continued] it is fulfilled without doubt. This is of the same kind as ﴿I answer the call of the caller when he calls upon Me﴾ (al-Baqarah: 186). In it there is a great incitement to supplication and a great encouragement toward being answered, as He, may He be exalted, promised in ﴿I answer the call of the caller﴾ (al-Baqarah: 186) and ﴿Call upon Me, I will respond to you﴾ (Ghafir: 60). Even if the supplicant does not see the fulfilment, the matter is as related by Imam Ahmad, al-Bazzar, and Abu Ya'la al-Mundhiri, with good chains of narration, and al-Hakim, who said: "its chain is sound," from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "No Muslim makes a supplication in which there is no sin or severing of kinship ties, except that Allah gives him one of three things: either He grants him his supplication, or He stores it up for him in the Hereafter, or He averts from him an evil equal to it." They said: "Then we shall make many supplications." He said: "Allah is more abundant [in giving]."

Al-Hakim also related from Jabir, may Allah be pleased with him, from the Prophet (ﷺ) who said: "On the Day of Resurrection Allah will call the believer and make him stand before Him, and He will say: 'My servant! I commanded you to call upon Me, and I promised you that I would respond to you. Did you call upon Me?' He will say: 'Yes, O Lord!' He will say: 'Indeed, you did not call upon Me with a supplication except that I responded to you. Did you not call upon Me on such and such a day, for a distress that had descended upon you, that I might relieve you of it, and I relieved you?' He will say: 'Yes, O Lord!' He will say: 'I hastened it for you in the world. And you called upon Me on such and such a day, for a distress that had descended upon you, that I might relieve you of it, but you did not see relief?' He will say: 'Yes, O Lord!' He will say: 'I have stored up for you in the Garden such and such.' And you called upon Me for a need that I would fulfil for you on such and such a day, and I fulfilled it?' He will say: 'Yes, O Lord!' He will say: 'I hastened it for you in the world. And you called upon Me on such and such a day for a need that I would fulfil for you, but you did not see its fulfilment?' He will say: 'Yes, O Lord!' He will say: 'I have stored up for you in its place in the Garden such and such.'" The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "So Allah does not leave any supplication that His believing servant made except that He makes clear to him either that it was hastened for him in the world or that it was stored up for him in the Hereafter. Then the believer will say at that station: 'Would that none of his supplications had been hastened for him!'"

Ibn Hibban in his Sahih, and al-Hakim, who said: "its chain is sound," related from Anas, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Do not be weak in supplication, for no one will perish while supplicating."

At-Tirmidhi and al-Hakim related from Abu Hurairah, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Call upon Allah while you are certain of being answered."

Al-Bukhari, Muslim, Abu Dawud, at-Tirmidhi, and Ibn Majah related from Abu Hurairah, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "One of you will be answered so long as he does not hasten, saying: 'I supplicated, but I was not answered.'" In a narration of Muslim and at-Tirmidhi: "A servant will continue to be answered so long as he does not supplicate for a sin or the severing of kinship ties, so long as he does not become hasty." It was asked: "O Messenger of Allah! What is hastiness?" He said: "He says: 'I have supplicated, but I have not been answered,' so he grows weary at that and abandons supplication." Al-Mundhiri said: "yastahsir" means he becomes bored and tired and so abandons supplication. End.

It is understood from the verse and from the hadith, in the exception of sin and the severing of kinship ties, that whatever there is no obstacle to asking for is one whose granting and bestowal are promised, so let a person supplicate for it while certain of being answered.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 25, verse 17:

When He had mentioned their condition on the Hour in relation to Himself, He followed it with mention of their condition in relation to the things they worship besides Him. He said, shifting to the manifestation of majesty according to the recitation of the majority: ﴿And [mention] the day﴾, that is, say to them what I have commanded you, and mention to them the day ﴿when He will gather them﴾, that is, the polytheists, by the majesty that We possess, which We will manifest on that day, ﴿from the graves﴾. Abu Ja'far, Ibn Kathir, Ya'qub, and Hafs from 'Asim read it with the yā' (third person), so the pronoun refers to the Lord. ﴿And those they worship﴾, that is, from among the angels, humans, jinn, and others, those who have intellect and those who do not. He drew attention to the lowliness of their rank relative to that and their unfitness for it by His words: ﴿besides Allah﴾, that is, the Supreme King who has no equal. He mentioned them with the word "mā" to indicate that their speaking and their silent ones are inanimate, indeed non-existent in relation to Him, glorified is He, as indicated by the expression with the greatest name (al-ism al-a'zam, the Name that encompasses all perfection). Yet "mā" is general in usage for rational and non-rational beings, although its most common usage is for non-rational beings. He, glorified is He, expressed it by His words: ﴿then He will say﴾, with the return of the third-person pronoun after the expression with the plural of majesty in "naḥshuru" in the recitation other than that of Ibn 'Amir, because the noble Name had preceded, to establish the intended meaning and make it explicit, and to inform that what is intended by the "nūn" is majesty, not plurality. Ibn 'Amir read it with the "nūn" maintaining a single style: ﴿"You"﴾, that is, O you objects of worship!, with the interrogative hamza placed before the pronoun, asking about the one who misled, because the misguidance of the worshippers is well known and is not asked about: ﴿Did you mislead﴾ by coercion, deception, and cunning ﴿these My servants﴾, until they worshipped you, as in the other verse:

﴿Then He will say to the angels, "Did these people used to worship you?"﴾ [Saba': 40], and similar verses, as in the sacred hadith (ḥadīth qudsī, a hadith in which the words are attributed to God): "Indeed I created My servants as ḥanīf (upright in pure monotheism), all of them, and then the devils led them astray." ﴿Or﴾

Since the question, as has passed, concerns the agent and not the act, it was necessary to say: ﴿they themselves﴾, that is, by their own choice, because they neglected to use what I had given them of upright intellect and sound reasoning, ﴿went astray﴾. He connected the verb without "ʿan" (from), as in "hudāt al-ṭarīq" (guides of the road) without "ilā" (to), because of its frequent occurrence, and to indicate the strength of the verb. So He said: ﴿the way﴾, that is, the one You laid out and upon which You set the decisive proofs and the shining demonstrations.

﴿They say﴾ — that is, the things worshipped, both the living among them and the inanimate, the obedient and the disobedient: ﴿Glory be to You!﴾ — that is, You are exalted above having any power over any action attributed to anyone other than You.

Since this glorification yields that there is no act of anyone other than Him, glory be to Him, they express this by their saying: ﴿It was not for us to take﴾ — that is, it is not valid or conceivable — ﴿to take﴾ — that is, to strive to adopt by our own choice, without any will from You — ﴿besides You﴾, and everything other than You is "besides You" — ﴿any allies﴾ — that is, who would benefit us. For we are in need of one who benefits us, because of our necessity and poverty. How then could we abandon the One in whose hand is everything, who is nearer to us in every sense of the meanings of ​​guardianship (wilayah), in knowledge, power and other things, than the one in whose hand is nothing, who is the furthest of the far in every sense of the meanings of guardianship? Even if we undertook to make Him near, He would not be so. This expression is apt whether those worshipped were righteous among the servants, such as prophets and angels, or others. If they were of the righteous, its meaning is: it was not fitting for us to do that, so we did not do it, and You know best, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿It is not for a human being that Allah should give him the Scripture and wisdom and prophethood and then he should say to the people...﴾ [Al 'Imran: 79], the verse. If they were inanimate things, the meaning is: we were not in the category of those who have power over any of that, but they did it out of insolence. If they were like Pharaoh (Fir'awn), the meaning is: this was not for us, but they brought us to this rank merely by their calling upon us, as Iblis says — ﴿And I had no authority over you except that I invited you, and you responded﴾ [Ibrahim: 22] — and that is because they did not reflect on the realities of matters. Thus on that Day they will all submit to Allah, so it is established that they were not in that rank to which they elevated them. The benefit of the question, despite the comprehensiveness of His knowledge, is to rebuke the obstinate, to increase their regret and remorse, and to make the believers rejoice when they hear this answer, in addition to the profound admonition in relating it to us. The reading of Abu Ja'far with the passive form, with a damma on the nun and a fatha on the kha', is clear in meaning, that is: He takes us as one of the gods whose affairs we manage.

Since the meaning is: "We did not lead them astray" — as for the case where it is assumed to be of the angels and the like, it is clear; and as for others, the one who truly leads astray is Allah, while outwardly it is their insolence toward the blessing and their following of desires, which kept them from deep reflection and held them to outward appearances. The transition with His saying ﴿But﴾ is apt — that is, we did not lead them astray, rather they went astray by Your will, because You ﴿gave them and their fathers enjoyment﴾ in the worldly life through what You lead them on with of subtle favors, and You prolonged their lives in that, ﴿until they forgot the Reminder﴾, which is not fitting to be called "the Reminder" except for something else, namely faith in all that You, glory be to You, sent Your messengers with, by proof that every intelligent person knows from his own self through the natural instinct of reason which You bestowed, that it is possible in some way that the God is only One. Between the intelligent person and remembering this there is only slight reflection, along with freedom from the taints of selfish interests. The sum is that You provided them with means through which they could not be guided, so You are the King, the Doer of what You will; none acts but You. ﴿And they were﴾ in Your knowledge of what You had decreed for them from eternity ﴿a people lost﴾, perished.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 25, verse 19:

Since this was a matter that was certainly going to happen, He turned to them in rebuke and said, using the past tense after the emphatic and confirming "qad": ﴿Then they will have denied you﴾, meaning the objects of worship denied the worshippers, because they had surrendered (*ilqa' al-silm*, "throwing down submission") and this requires that they do not deserve worship and that they intercede for you while subdued and under the control of a Lord. ﴿With what﴾, meaning because of what, ﴿you say﴾, O worshippers, that they deserve to be worshipped, that they will intercede for you, and that they led you astray. In the recitation of Ibn Kathir with the *ya'* of the third person (*al-tahtaniyya*), the meaning is: with what the objects of worship say of glorifying God and submitting, in your claim that they led you astray.

Since their surrender and their abandonment of those who worshipped them resulted in their having no benefit or harm in their hands, He said: ﴿So you cannot﴾, meaning the objects of worship, ﴿avert﴾ (*sarfan*) anything from anyone among people, neither you nor anyone else, of punishment or otherwise, by way of any stratagem, intercession, or ransom, ﴿nor achieve help﴾ (*nasran*) by overpowering. This is like His saying, ﴿So they have no power to remove the harm from you or to change it﴾ [al-Isra: 56].

Since the implied sense was: whoever among you turns away from hearing this admonition, by placing worship in its proper place, We will reward him with a great reward, He followed it with what the context requires, and said: ﴿And whoever among you wrongs﴾ by placing worship in other than its proper place, and by holding about the messengers what is not fitting, namely that they should not be like people in eating or in seeking sustenance and the like, ﴿We will make him taste﴾ in this world and the Hereafter, by virtue of Our greatness, ﴿a great punishment﴾.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 25, verse 20:

When Allah, glorified is He, had refuted what they had slandered His Messenger ﷺ with, and mentioned what He had recompensed them for it, and what He had prepared for them, for him, and for his followers, and had negated what they claimed about their deities, and concluded it with the punishment of the wrongdoer, He mentioned what they had wronged in by their saying ﴿What is this Messenger?﴾ [al-Furqan: 7] and the like. So He clarified that what they had made into a stain upon his character is the sunnah (way/practice) of Allah, glorified is He, regarding the messengers before him, as an example for their human kind. He followed this with its secret, and said, increasing in consolation, comfort and reassurance: ﴿And We did not send﴾ with what We have of majesty. Since the intended meaning is generality, He removed it from the preposition and said: ﴿before you﴾, i.e., O Muhammad, anyone ﴿among the messengers, except that﴾ and their condition was that ﴿they surely ate food﴾ as you eat, and others of the children of Adam eat, ﴿and walked in the markets﴾ as you do and they do, i.e., except that their condition was eating and walking to seek livelihood, like the condition of the rest of the children of Adam. And they knew this from what they had heard of their reports. This is an affirmation from Allah, exalted is He, for they do not deny him, upon him be blessings and peace, nor do they believe any deficiency in him. It is also a refutation of their argument by what they said of that, and an establishment of the proof against their obstinacy, and that they say it and its like only because of the firm rooting of denial of the Hour within themselves. ﴿And We have made﴾, i.e., by giving and withholding, with what We have of majesty, ﴿some of you a trial for others﴾, by making this one a prophet and specifying him with messengerhood, and this one a king and specifying him with worldly things, and this one a poor man and depriving him of worldly things, so that there may become manifest what We know of each of obedience and disobedience in the world of the unseen, to people in the world of witnessing. Thus We test the poor man by his patience over what he has been deprived of, compared to what the rich man has been given, or by his impatience; and the king, and whoever is in his meaning among the nobles, by their patience over what the Messenger has been given of honour and attaining closeness to Allah, to a level they cannot reach, despite what they are in of majesty. For this reason, I did not give My Messenger the world, and made him among those who choose servitude and sufficiency through seeking livelihood in the markets, so that I might test you in obedience to him sincerely. For if I had given him the world, and made him among those who choose kingship, the majority would have hastened to follow him out of greed for the world. This is the meaning of ﴿Will you be patient?﴾, for it is the cause of what precedes it, i.e., so that We may know with knowledge of witnessing whether you will be patient in what We have tested you with, or not, just as We know it with knowledge of the unseen, so that the proof may be established against you in the course of your customs. Along with its causality, there is in it an eloquent warning for whoever reflects. It is also permissible that the interrogative be a resumptive (new) sentence for warning.

Since the testing might give the impression of a deficiency in knowledge, and since His beneficence, glorified is He, to all creation was less than His beneficence to their master and essence, their pith and adornment, Muhammad ﷺ, and since He knew them to be the most aware of His transcendence and exaltation, and since testing them by making him a prophet and servant, while he was in the utmost honour with Him, might have led them to consider it humiliation, He negated what might give such an impression, both the interrogative and the testing, regarding the right of Allah, glorified is He, and the right of His prophet ﷺ, turning the address toward him, saying: ﴿And your Lord was﴾, i.e., the One who is beneficent to you with a beneficence He did not show to anyone other than you, especially by making you a prophet and servant, ﴿All-Seeing﴾ of everything. So He knows the human being before the testing; that knowledge did not give Him a knowledge He did not already have. He, glorified is He, places matters in the very center of their proper places, even if others see otherwise. Therefore it is incumbent upon every person to submit to Him in all matters, for that leads to great good, and to reflect upon His words and deeds with good submission and receiving, for that leads to abundant knowledge. He did not intend, by testing you with them and testing them with you in this great harm, except to elevate your station and lower their affair. ﴿And you will surely know its news after a time﴾ [Sad: 88].

When He mentioned this trial, after having mentioned at the beginning of the surah the greatness that He, glorified is He, possesses, namely the vastness of His dominion, the abundance of His works, and His beneficence towards all creation, and since it is the right of every creature under His nurture to come to know its Lord, whoever it may be, especially when He is described by this attribute, so that it may obtain of His beneficence and be strengthened by Him over its peers, He followed that by exposing the trial, showing that they have no insight. So He said, exalted is He: ﴿And said﴾, and He made explicit, in the place of the pronoun, the description that was earlier stated to be the cause of their blindness, so He said: ﴿Those who do not expect to meet Us﴾, that is, they have no intellects, because they have forgotten ﴿Our meeting﴾. Thus they do no deed by which they hope for Our confirming them in it after death, in light of what they know of Our greatness, which whoever hopes for, it becomes his, and he is made happy, and whoever turns away from it, it becomes against him, and he is destroyed. Their intellects have therefore become subservient to their desires, so they come to know inanimate things which they call their lords, and they seek them out and seek blessing from them, hoping for the impossible and immersing themselves in error. So He mentioned "hope" for this purpose, although it necessarily entails the absence of fear: ﴿Why not?﴾ That is, why did they not, and why would it not be so?

When their aim, through their ignorance, was that they should see them all at once, He expressed it with the verb "to send down" and said: ﴿Were sent down﴾, that is, in whatever manner and from whatever source, ﴿upon us the angels﴾, that is, just as they were sent down upon him, as he claims, ﴿or we see our Lord﴾ with what He has of beneficence towards us, and what we have of greatness through strength, through wealth and other things, so that He would command us as He wishes without need of an intermediary.

Since this statement is one that no human should dare to make, because in it there is an objection against the One whose greatness cannot be described and whose wisdom's purposes cannot be grasped, He began with the particle of expectation (harf al-tawaqqu'), in response to what the context guided to, as an answer to one who seems to have asked: what is their state in this? ﴿Indeed﴾, that is, by Our might, indeed ﴿they have become arrogant﴾, that is, they sought arrogance, rather they brought arrogance into existence. Since their arrogance had no visible fruit, because it does not return harm upon anyone other than themselves, He said: ﴿within themselves﴾, that is, by seeking to see the angels.

Since the sum of their matter is that they sought the rank of the Prophet, whose intermediary is an angel, and they added to it the seeking of seeing all the angels who receive from Allah, and they went further by seeking to see [Allah Himself], He said: ﴿and have transgressed﴾, that is, they exceeded the limit in arrogance by what lies beyond it, namely their seeking to see all the angels and to see the Sovereign, the Almighty. And He emphasized this meaning further, as the context required, by His saying: ﴿a great transgression﴾. And the clarification that they only said this out of transgression and wrongdoing is that what came to them of signs, the greatest of which is the Qur'an, had definitively shown them their inability to produce anything like it, [proving] its truthfulness, (ﷺ), regarding Allah in all that he says. And in the excellence of this resumptive sentence (isti'naf) and in the implication of this context there is an indication of wonder, without the use of any word of wonder. The meaning is: how intense is their arrogance, and how great their transgression!

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 25, verse 22:

Then he (Allah) explained to them their condition at the time of some of what they had asked for, saying: ﴿On the Day﴾ — its governing element is what is indicated by "no good tidings" (lā bushrā) — ﴿when they see the angels﴾, that is, on the Day of Resurrection, or before it in the battles, or at the time of death (al-iḥtiḍār), ﴿there will be no good tidings﴾, that is, good tidings of any kind at all, ﴿on that Day for the criminals﴾, that is, for anyone among those who severed what Allah commanded to be joined. And to clarify this, he made the explicit noun appear in place of the pronoun (al-iḍmār). ﴿And they will say﴾, that is, at that time: ﴿"A forbidding, forbidden"﴾ — that is, we seek a barrier, a forbidding barrier, from you, meaning one that is emphatically forbidding. It is also permissible that the passive form (al-maf'ūl) be understood as the active (al-fā'il), and the meaning is the same: they wish that there be between them and the angels a great barrier that prevents them from them. Abū ʿUbayda said: This is the ʿawdha (refuge-cry) of the Arabs, which a person says when he fears another within the Sacred Precinct (al-Ḥaram) or in a sacred month, when he meets him and there is a blood-feud (tirah) between them. Sībawayh said: he means disavowal of the matter and keeping far from himself something; it is as if he said: "I forbid that, a forbidden prohibition." Similar to this is when a man says to another: "Will you do such-and-such?" and he replies: "Ḥijran," meaning a screen and disavowal of this. This is in the accusative by the implied verb (iḍmār al-fi'l).

He used the present tense (yaqūlūn) to indicate the continuity of their renewing this statement after being startled by it at the moment of seeing them, due to their great terror of them, unlike what follows it, where he used the past tense to indicate that it is certain to occur.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 25, verse 23:

When the one who wishes to nullify a thing, out of his intense aversion to it, is not content to nullify it through anything other than himself, but comes to it personally and nullifies it, He expressed it with His saying: ﴿And We will proceed﴾ (wa-qadimna), that is, with the overwhelming majesty We possess, on that Day in which they see the angels, whether in this world or in the Hereafter, ﴿to what they did of deeds﴾, that is, of noble character (makarim al-akhlaq) (p-371) such as generosity (al-jud), maintaining the ties of kinship (silat al-rahim), forbearance (al-hilm), courage in doing good (al-najda fi al-khayr), relieving the distressed (ighathat al-malhuf), and other such things, ﴿and We will make it﴾ (fa-ja'alnahu), because it was not founded upon faith, but was for the sake of desire and Satan, ﴿scattered dust﴾ (habaan), meaning void, with no benefit in it. This is the meaning of ﴿habaan﴾, which is what is seen in the sunlight entering through a window, resembling dust. It is thus the most like nothingness, because it has no benefit at all.

Since the habaa is seen when still, arranged in order, but when the wind stirs it, it scatters and goes in every direction, most of its entry into the realm of non-existence occurs even though it is perceptible. He said, in emphasizing the description of their deeds: ﴿scattered﴾ (manthuran), which is a description (sifa). It has also been said that it is a third object (maf'ul thalith) of ja'ala, meaning: We made their deeds comprehensive of the insignificance of dust and of being scattered.

Since he knew from this that the implied meaning is: "They are in such a state that they have no resting place, when the Fire is their abode," he followed it with the opposite condition, saying: ﴿The companions of the Garden on that Day are better in their dwelling-place﴾, that is, on the day when they see the angels, ﴿and better in their resting-place﴾, that is, a place suitable for settling, due to its goodness, and they will be settled in it for most of their time, reclining on couches, facing one another, conversing. This is a sign that the abode of those people cannot be settled in. (p-372) ﴿And finer in resting﴾, that is, a place where one can rest at the time of the midday rest, to relax with their spouses and enjoy what happens in privacy. It is narrated that the time of reckoning, despite its length, will be shortened for the believers until it is like the period between the beginning of the day and the time of the midday rest, so they will take their midday rest in the gardens of Paradise until people finish the reckoning.

He used the comparative form (af'al al-tafdil) as mockery of them, or because the speech was general, covering the conditions of this world and the Hereafter, while they were certain that in this world they were in a better state than the believers, due to their abundance of wealth, plenty, and strength. By the word "goodness" (husn) there is an indication of what their resting-place is adorned with, such as beauty of faces, comeliness of forms, and the like.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (*Nazm al-Durar*) on surah 25, verse 25:

When the disbelievers, in this abode, enjoy such might, strength, and grandeur that they marvel at the outcome of their state and the state of their adversaries, as mentioned, He made clear that the matter on that Day is not as we are accustomed to it. So He said, conjoining it to ﴿On the Day they see﴾ [al-Furqan: 22] ﴿and the Day the sky is split open﴾, meaning a great splitting, although there is some obscurity in this for some people, as indicated by the deletion of its *ta'* (the feminine marker in *tashaqqaqu*, i.e., the verb is read as *tashaqqaqu* with one *ta'* elided). ﴿With clouds﴾, meaning, just as the earth is split open by plants so that they emerge through its cracks. He also pointed to the ignorance of those who asked for their descent all at once, by His words: ﴿And the angels are sent down﴾, meaning gradually, by a decree that is binding and that they cannot evade, by the command of the One who has no command over anyone else, ﴿descending﴾ (the angels who asked to be seen in one state), (p. 373) ﴿in a descent﴾, with scrolls of deeds in their hands.

Ibn ʿAbbas (may Allah be pleased with him and his father) said: The sky is split open in this world, and its inhabitants descend, and they are more numerous than the jinn and humans in this world. Then the second sky is split open, and its inhabitants descend, and they are more numerous than the inhabitants of the first sky and the people of the earth, jinn and humans. Then so on, until the seventh sky is split open. The inhabitants of each sky exceed the inhabitants of the sky before it. Then the Kurubiyyun (the cherubim) descend, then the bearers of the Throne.

The Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on Surah 25, verse 26:

When that day became a cause for the disclosure of matters and for knowing that there is no sovereignty for anyone other than Him, glory be to Him, because none other than He judges on it, He said: ﴿The sovereignty on that day﴾, meaning the day when the sky is split open with the clouds. Then He described the sovereignty with His words: ﴿the true﴾, meaning its meaning is firmly established, with a firmness whose removal is impossible. Then He informed about it with His words: ﴿belongs to the Most Merciful (al-Rahman)﴾, meaning the One whose mercy is general in both abodes. Among the generality of His mercy and the truth of His sovereignty is that He gladdens the hearts of the people of His love by punishing the people of His enmity, who opposed them regarding it, because of their squandering of the truth by following falsehood. Were it not for His attribute of mercy, no one would enter Paradise. The meaning of the construction is that the sovereignty of anyone else on that day is only in the name by which he was previously named in this world, only that, with no rule for him at all, neither inwardly nor outwardly, as it was in this world. ﴿And it was﴾, meaning that day on which the angels appear, whose sight the disbelievers had requested (p-374), ﴿a difficult day for the disbelievers﴾, meaning only for them, ﴿hard﴾, extremely difficult and grievous.

When the overall state of these people was that they had shunned the noblest of creation, who guided them to every good, and had befriended others who would lead them to every evil, He explained the severity of that Day. Their audacity in denying it was caused only by the extreme regret they would feel for this conduct. He said: ﴿And the day the wrongdoer will bite on his hands﴾, i.e., out of excessive grief at what he sees of its terrors, ﴿on his hands﴾, i.e., both of them, so that he nearly cuts them off from the intensity of his remorse, while being unaware of it. Along with this action, ﴿he will say﴾, i.e., he will renew in every moment his saying: ﴿Oh, would that I had taken﴾, i.e., would that I had compelled myself and obliged myself to take, in the worldly life, ﴿with the Messenger a way﴾, i.e., one single deed from among the deeds to which he called me, and that I had obeyed him with some obedience, because of what was revealed to me on this Day, that whoever obeyed him, even for a moment, attained happiness in proportion to that. Biting the hand and the fingertips, and gnashing the teeth, and the like, are a kināyah (metonymy) for rage and regret, because they are among the concomitants (radīfah) of these two.
