So the concomitant is mentioned as an indication of what it accompanies, and the speech thereby rises in the rank of fasāhah (eloquence) to a degree at which the listener finds in himself, on hearing it, a sense of awe and admiration that he does not find in the case of the one referred to by the plain expression.

(p-375) When he (the disbeliever) regretted having shunned the Messenger, he lamented over having taken others as close companions, saying: ﴿Woe is me!﴾ That is, "O my ruin, for I have no companion other than him, since there is no one in my presence besides him." Since he was wishing for something impossible, he expressed it with its particle, saying: ﴿Would that I had not taken so-and-so﴾ meaning the one who led him astray, whom he does not name by his name. Rather, He (glory be to Him), Who fears no opposition and has no need of flattery, referred to him indirectly, intending generality, even though the verse was revealed concerning a specific person. ﴿As a friend﴾ meaning a companion whose deeds I would follow, because of what I knew of their evil outcome.

Then he resumed his statement, which every hearer would expect him to make: ﴿Indeed﴾, that is, by God, indeed ﴿he led me astray from the Reminder﴾, that is, he obscured for me the path of the Qur'an, which in reality is no reminder other than it, and turned me away from it. The clause stands in the position of a causal explanation for what precedes it: ﴿after it had come to me﴾, and there was no evident obstacle preventing me from it other than his misguiding me.

Since the implied sense is: "Then here he has forsaken me, when I was most in need of his support," he attached to it his statement: ﴿And Satan is ever a forsaker to man﴾, that is, every one who is a cause of misguidance, from the stubborn among the jinn and mankind, ﴿a forsaker to man﴾, that is, extremely forsaking: he leads him into harm and then delivers him to the most hateful of what he dislikes, not supporting him. Even if he wished to, he would not be able to; rather, he is worse than that, for upon him is his own sin and the like of the sin of whoever he misled.

[p-376] When He, glory be to Him, had mentioned the statements of the disbelievers, concluding with their being led astray from the Reminder, and while they were, together with their display of denial of it and their claim that it was fabricated, in extreme delight with it, swayed by it, amazed by it, and aware that it would have a momentous outcome, He indicated this in His saying, linking it to ﴿And they say, "What is wrong with this Messenger?"﴾ [al-Furqan: 7]. This magnifies the complaint made against him ﷺ, and it is a warning to his people, because the messengers before him, peace be upon them, whenever their peoples disbelieved, had a punishment of total destruction (isti'sal) sent down upon those peoples. ﴿And the Messenger said﴾, meaning Muhammad ﷺ: ﴿"O my Lord"﴾, O You who have shown me kindness in its many forms, the greatest of which is the Message. He used the particle of distance (ya' of distance) in addressing Him, to humble himself and as an intensification of supplication. ﴿"Indeed, my people"﴾, i.e., the Quraysh, who have power, standing and protection, ﴿"have taken"﴾, i.e., by forcing themselves against what they find in it, ﴿"this Qur'an"﴾, i.e., which calls for gathering around it and hastening to it, ﴿"as something abandoned"﴾, i.e., forsaken. By the form of the reflexive measure (ifti'al, the verbal form that adds the infix -ta- and signifies effort or self-directed action), He indicated that they exerted themselves greatly in abandoning it, because of the beauty of its composition that they perceived, the sweetness of its meanings that they tasted, its exquisite methods, its subtle marvels, and its wondrous rarities. This is known from the story of Abu Jahl, Abu Sufyan ibn Harb and al-Akhnas ibn Shariq, when they used to listen to its recitation at night, each one in a place where his two companions did not know of him. Then the road gathered them when they woke in the morning, and they reproached one another and made a pact not to return. Then they returned [p-377] and did this for three nights, after which they reinforced their oaths upon themselves until they gave it up, as is well known in the biographies (sirah).

When this speech carried the sense of complaint, intense burning, and great grief, as indicated by the use of *yā* (O), which is for distance, contrary to the customary way of calling the elite, whom he is most special to, and the questioning about the reason for their abandonment despite their having incentives toward it, it was as if it were said: That is because the one who did this opposed you out of envy for you. And he connected to it: ﴿And thus﴾, i.e., and like what We did of this great act, while you are the greatest of creation before Us, ﴿We appointed﴾ by what We have of greatness, ﴿for every prophet﴾, i.e., of the prophets before you, elevation for their ranks, ﴿an enemy from among the criminals﴾ who We have made inclined to cutting off what requires connection, so We misguided them thereby as humiliation for them. So be patient as they were patient, for I will guide through you whom I will, and help you against others, and honor your people from the punishment of extermination, as an honoring of you.

When it was a station where souls are attached, longing for guidance after this sealing, and for victory after that appointing, it was as if it were said: Do not grieve, for We will surely make for you a friend from among those We guide to faith, and We will surely help them against their enemy as We did with those before you, (p-٣٧٨) rather greater, until We subdue their nations from that wonder, and they will have no choice but submission to you and entering into the shade of your might. And since that, because of the multitude of opponents, is a matter that merits astonishment, he said, conjoining to what is implied: Then He helped your brethren among the prophets, peace be upon them, against those whom their Lord, who sent them, made their enemies: ﴿And sufficient is your Lord﴾, i.e., the one who does good to you, ﴿as a guide﴾, guiding through you whom He has decreed happiness for, ﴿and a helper﴾, helping you against whom He has decreed wretchedness.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 25, verse 32:

When He, glory be to Him, mentioned His complaint about their abandonment of the Qur'an, and established their enmity toward it and His support of it against them, He followed that with what indicates it, saying, coupling it to what had passed of the similar ones in doubts, and making the place of the pronoun manifest to draw attention to the attribute that moved them to this statement: ﴿And those who disbelieved said﴾, meaning they concealed, out of enmity and envy, what their intellects bear witness to the soundness of, namely that the Qur'an is speech which is miraculous to them, individually revealed, let alone as a whole; and they concealed what had become clear to them of its manifest signs, which testify to His oneness, and other of its lofty attributes. ﴿Why not﴾, meaning "why is it not that".

Since they, because of the severity of their weakness, scarcely allowed themselves to call the Qur'an "revelation", let alone attribute its sending down to God, glory be to Him and exalted, they used the passive form in this objection which they raised, saying: ﴿It has been sent down to him﴾. And since they expressed it with the form of taf'il (intensive/repetitive form), which indicates gradualness and separation, to attract the listener so that he would not turn away from them, they indicated that this was not what they intended, and so they said: ﴿the Qur'an﴾, meaning whose name necessarily implies collection; then they stated the intended meaning explicitly with their saying: ﴿all at once﴾, and they emphasized it with their saying: ﴿in one go﴾, meaning from its beginning to its end in a single time, so that it would be established that it is from God, and what we suppose to be removed from us, namely that it is he who arranges it little by little. Thus their expression by what indicates separation is more eloquent for their purpose, for they made the listener eager to attend to their speech by settling him upon what approaches their aim, then they removed it gradually to the utmost removal, so there was in that, through the surprise of dismay and the despair of what had been hoped for from approximation, what was not in "anzala" (sent down). And God knows best.

Since the intended sense was: "And why is it not sent down to him in separate parts," and since separation has great benefits, He, glory be to Him, indicated its greatness with His saying, expressing by the distal demonstrative the indication to the greatness it comprises: ﴿Thus﴾, meaning We sent it down piece by piece in this magnificent manner which they denied, ﴿that We may strengthen your heart thereby﴾, by aid, through the repeated coming of messengers between us and you, and by enabling you and your followers to comprehend the meanings, and by lightening the rulings in imposing them upon the people of Islam, gradually according to what is beneficial, and because of the wisdom in abrogating and abrogated rulings, due to the benefits arranged in it, and to facilitate memorization, especially since the community was unlettered, neither reading nor writing, and to provide answers at their times, and to magnify the miraculous nature, for whatever he challenged them with a portion of it and they were unable, they knew that inability regarding more of it is more certain. The conclusion is that separation is more admissible within the domain of inimitability, and in each there is wisdom. Thus it is known that this objection is superfluous and disputation over what has no benefit, arising from narrowness of wits, scarcity of ornament, and the distress of error, the habit of one cut off and confounded; for the basis is inimitability, and as for whether it was sent all at once or in separate parts, this is a matter in which they have no benefit. The indication is not capable of referring to the earlier books, because their revelation was only in installments, as I explained in Surat al-Nisa' from the text of the Torah which our Book's text indicates, not as many people imagine, and it has no basis except a lie from some Jews, by which they cast doubt upon the people of Islam, and it spread among most of them, and they began to labor to produce answers to it. The Jews now acknowledge that the Torah was revealed over about twenty years. And God is the Granter of success.

Since its sending down in separate parts was better, He emphasized it with His saying, coupling it to the verb to which "thus" is attached: ﴿and We have arranged it in arrangement﴾, meaning We separated it in its sending down to you, in separation over twenty-odd years. Al-Baghawi said: Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, said: "We made it clear with clarity," and tartil is distinctness in measured and steady recitation, ended. Its origin is the arrangement of the teeth, which is their being spaced apart like the bloom of the chamomile.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 25, verse 33:

Since the implied sense was: "What they brought forward as this objection has been nullified," he followed it with His saying: ﴿And they do not bring you any parable﴾, that is, the polytheists do not bring you any objection aimed at nullifying your affair, by which they seek to delude the minds of the weak, striving to embellish it, refine it and polish it until it appears to them to be at the utmost degree of beauty and elegance, in wording and in meaning, ﴿except that We bring you the truth﴾, that is, in reply to it. From the alif and lam, which indicate perfection, it is known that what is meant by "the truth" is that which is firmest, such that nothing is firmer than it. Thus what they brought is overwhelmed by its falsehood, and after that concealment it is exposed to a disgrace that shames both the speaker and the receptive listener.

Since the implied sense originally was: "with something more true than it," and He expressed it only as "the truth" so that it would not be understood that what they bring has any real standing, He followed it with His saying: ﴿and better in explanation﴾, that is, better than their parable, in unveiling what had covered understanding from that which they had made appear and claimed to have clarified, as a face of the faces of their slanders; so most of the listeners were certain of its excellence.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 25, verse 34:

When all these verses had established that they are obstinate toward their Lord, and that they intend by these questions to lead His way astray, to belittle His station, and to disregard His rank, (p-382) it was known with certainty that He would fill the abode of wretchedness with them. This was the clearest proof that they are the most blind of people to the perceptible paths, let alone to well-known examples and to the illustration of obscure perceptions, and that they are the basest of people, for none belittles the excellent except a deficient person, and a person speaks only about one who is better than himself. In response to His saying ﴿The companions of the Garden on that Day are better﴾ [al-Furqan: 24], He said, describing what preceded, that He placed the outward noun in the position of the pronoun in His saying "those who disbelieve": ﴿Those who will be gathered﴾, that is, they will be driven by force, walking upside down, ﴿upon their faces﴾, or dragged, ﴿to Hell﴾, just as in this world they used to act as though they were not seeing with Him, and had no control over their own selves, the devils urging them on with urging. For the Hereafter is the mirror of this world: whatever one does here is seen there, just as this world is the field of the Hereafter: whatever one sows in it, its fruit is harvested there. Al-Bukhari narrated from Anas, may Allah be pleased with him, that a man said: "O Prophet of Allah! How will the disbeliever be gathered upon his face on the Day of Resurrection?" He said: "Is not He who made him walk on his two feet in this world able to make him walk upon his face on the Day of Resurrection?" Qatadah said, meaning the narrator from Anas: "Yes, by the might of our Lord."

(p-383) When He described the captious ones regarding the matter of the Qur'an with this description, He resumed informing that they are characterized by what they were charged with, namely that bringing the Qur'an in installments is placing a thing in other than its proper place. So He said: ﴿Those﴾, that is, the remote and hateful, ﴿are worse﴾, that is, the worst of creation, ﴿in place and further astray in way﴾, in that they were blind to the path of the Garden, which has no clearer or wider path, and they took the path of the Fire, which has no narrower or more rugged path, and they were blind to the fact that sending down the Qur'an in stages is more fitting, because of the subtleties preceding it and others that none encompasses except Allah the Exalted. "And way" is a specifier transferred from the agent; its original form is: "their way went astray," and attributing the straying to it is a metaphorical attribution.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 25, verse 35:

When he had made clear that they denied him and opposed him, and had indicated through the verse of the gathering (al-hashr) toward Hell that He would not destroy them with a general destruction, he followed the governing element of "li-nuthabbita" (so that We may strengthen), as consolation for him and as a warning to them, with His saying: ﴿And We certainly gave Moses the Book﴾, that is, by the greatness that is ours, ﴿Moses the Book﴾, as We gave you (the Book). We made clear in it the laws (shara'i'), the ways (sunan) and the rulings (ahkam), and We made it a guidance and a mercy. We sent it down to him in installments over about twenty years, it is said eighteen, just as We sent down to you this Qur'an over a little more than twenty years, as I have explained in the end of Surat al-Nisa' and elsewhere. Moreover, anyone who has studied the Torah cannot deny this, for it is clear from its texts.

He added to the consolation by mentioning the minister (wazir), because the rejection of two is more remote. In it is also an indication that sending an angel, as they proposed, so that he might be a warner along with him, would not benefit them in faith. So He said: ﴿And We made﴾, by the greatness that is ours, ﴿with him his brother﴾, then He specified him by His saying: ﴿Harun (Aaron)﴾, and He specified the object of the appointment by His saying: ﴿a minister﴾, that is, a helper in every matter for which We sent him. And he, along with that, was a prophet, and there is no contradiction between being a minister and being a prophet.

Since the conjunction "wa" (and) does not indicate sequence, it does not follow from this that this appointment came after the descent of the Book, as is actually the case; so He followed it with His words: ﴿Then We said﴾, meaning: after We had appointed him as a minister.

Since the purpose of the story here is consolation and warning, He mentioned its outer parts, the first and the last, which are the establishing of proof and the destruction, so He said: ﴿Go to the people﴾, meaning those who have strength and power over what they inflict, and they are the Copts, ﴿who denied Our signs﴾, meaning the signs seen and heard from the earlier prophets before your coming, in the knowledge of witnessing, and the signs seen and heard from you two after your coming, in Our knowledge. So they went to them, and they denied them regarding what they showed them and informed them of from the signs, (p-385) because of the seal We had set upon them, the seal that prepared them for this.

Since the context is one of warning with the Criterion, He left aside their matter except regarding their punishment, so He said: ﴿Then We destroyed them﴾, meaning for that reason, ﴿with complete destruction﴾, by drowning them all at the hand of Moses, peace be upon him, in the sea, leaving none of them alive, along with the calamities We had already afflicted them with before that, and despite Moses' peace be upon him striving to give them life through faith, which would have necessitated their preservation in both abodes. This is the reverse of what We did with Moses, peace be upon him, in saving him from destruction by casting him into the sea and preserving him among those who had striven to destroy him. We also gave each of the two a portion of its sea: ﴿This one is salty, bitter﴾, which is the covering of Hell, and ﴿this one is sweet, palatable﴾, whose source is from Paradise. So let those whom you call to the like of that beware, should they do the like of what those did.

Al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 25, verse 37:

When He had threatened the deniers with the destruction of the earlier peoples, who were stronger than they and more numerous, and had put forward the story of Musa, peace be upon him, first because of the connection of the Book with him in himself, and secondly in its being revealed in stages (tanjim), He followed it with the first of the nations, because they were the first, and because of the terror in their punishment, and because of the connection between it and the punishment of the Copts. So He said: ﴿And the people of Nuh﴾, meaning: and We destroyed the people of Nuh ﴿when they denied the messengers﴾, by their denial of Nuh. For whoever denies one of the prophets in act has denied all of them in potential, because the miracles are the proof of their truthfulness, and they are equal in their footing as supernatural acts that no one can match; so denying any of them is denying all of them, since there is no difference. And also because they denied those prophets who had passed before them, peace and blessings be upon them, in what they had heard of their reports. And also because they gave as their reason for denying (Nuh) that he was a human being, so it followed that they denied every messenger who was a human being.

And since it was as if it were said: "By what were they destroyed?", He said: ﴿We drowned them﴾, just as We drowned the family of Pharaoh, with something greater than what We drowned them with, ﴿and We made them﴾, meaning the people of Nuh in that event, ﴿a sign for mankind﴾, meaning a marker of Our power over what We will, such as bringing forth water and other things, causing it to cease, and disposing of such matters in whatever way We wish, and saving whomever We will by means of that with which We destroyed their enemy. ﴿And We prepared﴾, meaning We readied with a very near preparation and presented in a mighty, severe manner of complete determination; the original would have been "for them", but He made it more general and tied the judgment to the attribute, so He said: ﴿for the wrongdoers﴾, meaning all of them at any time they existed, because of their wrongdoing by placing things in other than their proper places, ﴿a painful punishment﴾, especially in the Hereafter.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 25, verse 38:

When He mentioned the last and the first of the destroyed nations in general, and their destruction was by water, He mentioned among them those who were destroyed by other than that, to show His power and choice. He omitted the report about them, other than the punishment, because, as has passed in the context of warning, He said: ﴿And ʿĀd﴾, meaning, and We destroyed ʿĀd with the wind; ﴿and Thamūd﴾ with the Blast; ﴿and the companions of the Rass﴾, that is, the well, which is not covered over. Ibn Jarir said: "Al-Rass in the speech of the Arabs is every excavated thing, such as a well, a grave, and the like." That is, We destroyed them by the earth swallowing them up. ﴿And generations between that﴾, that is, between that great matter mentioned, and it is between every two nations of these nations, ﴿many﴾. And consider what the Most High, the Great, says about it: it is many. Al-Baghawi, in his tafsir of ﴿a justly balanced nation﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143] in al-Baqarah, transmitted from Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) stood among us one day after the ʿAsr prayer, and he did not leave anything until the Day of Resurrection without mentioning it in that position, until the sun was on the tops of the palm trees and the edges of the walls. He said: ‘Indeed, nothing remained of the world in what has passed except as much as remains of this day of yours. Know that this nation will outlive seventy nations, being the last of them and the most honoured of them before Allah, Mighty and Majestic.’" Al-Tirmidhī recorded it in the chapter on Trials, and Aḥmad, al-Ṭabarānī, and Ibn Mājah, also in the chapter on Trials, but only part of it; none of them has the intended wording about the seventy nations. In some of their wordings: "and we turned to look at the sun to see whether any of it remained." This indicates that what remained of the day was about a tenth of a tenth. This, if we consider what has passed of time for this nation, requires that what has passed of the world from the creation of Ādam (peace be upon him) on the Friday that follows the six days in which the heavens and the earth were created, is more than one hundred thousand years, and Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 25, verse 39:

When He (glory be to Him) had mentioned that He brings in this Book what is the truth in answer to their objections, He made clear that a similar treatment was meted out to all (the earlier nations). So He said, consoling His Prophet (ﷺ), giving him an example to follow, and showing the honour of his being granted pardon for his community: ﴿And each We struck with examples﴾, i.e., of these nations, ﴿by Our own might and majesty﴾, ﴿for him the parables﴾, until the way became clear to him and the proof was established beyond any doubt. ﴿And each We utterly destroyed with complete destruction﴾, i.e., We made them into crumbs, pieces cut into thorough fragments, such that none other than Us could join them together and restore them to what they were before being broken to pieces.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 25, verse 40:

(p-389) When he mentioned destruction by water and by other means, and destruction by water was sometimes by the sea and sometimes by rain, and he concluded with the sinking into the earth (khasf), he mentioned the sinking that arose from the rains, together with the stones of fire, along with being submerged in water, as an indication of the completeness of power and the striking greatness, and as a reminder of what they see every little while on their journey to the Holy Land for their trade. He opened the narrative with the lam (al-lam), which announces great concern, joined with the particle of confirmation (harf al-tahqiq), as an indication that they, because they did not benefit from the signs, were like those who deny what is perceived by the senses. He changed the style to draw attention to the great matter and to shake the listener, so he said: ﴿And they had certainly come﴾, that is, these deniers from your people, and he said: ﴿upon the town﴾ - even though it was seven or five cities, as has been said - belittling its status in comparison with His power, glorified is He, and humiliating for whoever wants His punishment, and as an indication of the gathering of the wickedness for them, until they were as though they were one thing, as indicated by the expression with the root "qaraa" which indicates gathering: ﴿which was rained upon﴾, that is, its raining occurred by One who has no power over raining except Him, with stones, and therefore He said: ﴿with the rain of evil﴾. They were the villages of the people of Lut. Then He sank them into the earth and they were submerged with what is not in the earth like it in kinds of wickedness. Al-Baghawi said: They were five villages, and Allah destroyed four of them and one survived, and it was the smallest of them, and its people (p-390) did not do the evil deed.

When they used to pass by them on their journeys, and it was their due that they should take warning from their state and turn back from their error, there resulted from that their deserving of severe denunciation in His saying: ﴿Had they not been seeing them?﴾, that is, with what is in their natures of lofty morals, ﴿seeing them﴾, that is, on their journeys to Syria, that they might take lesson from what befell their people of Allah's punishment and repent.

Since the estimation was: "Rather, they had seen them," he turned away from it with His saying: ﴿Rather﴾, that is, their denial was not because of not seeing them and not knowing what befell their people, but rather because ﴿they used to﴾ deny the Resurrection, as if it were a natural disposition for them.

Since a person's return to the health he had is beloved to him, it would have been fitting for them, had they reasoned, to hang their hope on the resurrection, because there is no return to life, so it is like the return of the sick to health, especially the one wasted by illness. Therefore He said, expressing it by hope, as an alert to this: ﴿They do not hope for a resurrection﴾ after death, so that they would fear Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and devote themselves sincerely to Him, and He would reward them for that, because the denial of the Hereafter had settled in their souls as a belief, and they persisted in it generation after generation, until it became so firmly established that no lesson benefits them with it except for whom Allah wills.

(p-391) Having established their denial of the Hereafter, he (God) followed it with a confirmation of it, explaining that they did not confine themselves to denying what is possible and desirable, but went so far as to add mockery of one who, by ordinary custom, could never be a fit object of ridicule at all: ﴿And when they see you﴾, that is, even though they know the truthfulness of your speech and the nobility of your conduct, had you not brought them a miracle, ﴿they take you not except in mockery﴾, that is, they do nothing but take you in mockery. He expressed it with the verbal noun (huzu) to indicate the extremity of their mockery, despite the great remoteness of the Prophet ﷺ from such a thing. They say in contempt: ﴿Is this the one whom God has sent as a messenger?﴾ They combined scorn with disbelief in their words ﴿the one whom God has sent﴾, meaning the one who embodies the attributes of greatness, ﴿as a messenger﴾. Thus, their putting the statement in the form of acceptance and affirmation, while it is in fact at the utmost degree of denial, reaches the peak of mockery. The meaning for them therefore becomes: this claim of his to prophethood is something that cannot be believed at all.

Then they resumed, vain of themselves, imagining that others would be distracted from attention to the miracles he brings. They said: ﴿Indeed he nearly﴾, that is, he almost, and it is known that "in" (إنْ) here is the light form (مُخَفَّفَةٌ, mukhaffafa, the lightened "inna") and not a negation with the lam, so he said: ﴿led us astray﴾, that is, by these supernatural acts which no one other than him can perform, and by his effort in showing sincere counsel, ﴿from our gods﴾, these gods to whose worship one better than us in judgment and more experienced in affairs had already preceded. Since this statement implied that they were close to being turned away from the idols, they negated it by their saying (p-٣٩٢): ﴿Had we not been steadfast in them﴾, through the gathering and mutual support we have, ﴿in them﴾, that is, in clinging to their worship.

Since this saying of theirs entails that the idols benefit them, He negated it while threatening them, and He emphasized the threat because of the enormity of their deed, in His saying, as a continuation of what is implied by the sense: "They will soon see — or whoever among them sees — that most of them have returned from the belief that these idols are gods": ﴿And they will soon know﴾, that is, in a state in which action will not benefit them, however long the period of respite and empowerment has been, ﴿when they see the punishment﴾, that is, in this world and in the Hereafter, ﴿who is further astray in the way﴾, whether they themselves or the one who called them to abandon the idols, whom they claimed to be misleading them by their saying ﴿he nearly led us astray﴾.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 25, verse 43:

When Allah, exalted is He, informed him of the reality of their state, both at their beginning and their end, and this was among the things that grieved him (ﷺ) because of his intense eagerness for their return and for their adherence to what benefits them and avoidance of what harms them, He consoled him by saying, marvelling at their state: ﴿Have you seen one who takes as his god his own desire?﴾ That is, he burdened himself by taking ﴿his god to be his desire﴾. That is, they have belittled the deity by lowering Him to the rank of desire, so they worship nothing but desire, and desire is the inclination of appetite and the impulse of the soul toward a thing. They have no doubt at all in worshipping idols; they would give it up if it were made clear. So they do not cease worshipping them as long as their desire exists, and none can restrain them from that except the One who is able to turn those desires away, and He is Allah alone. This is like when you say: "So-and-so has taken his companion to be his book," meaning that he has confined himself to conversing with the book, so he converses with no one but the book, though others may share with him in conversing with the book. But if you said: "He has taken his book as his companion," the situation would be reversed, and the meaning would be that he has confined himself to reading the companion and does not look into a book at the time of conversation, though others may share the companion with him. Or [it is like] confining the companion to the book and the book to the companion, just as you confine clay to pottery when you say: "I have made clay into pottery." So the meaning is that this blameworthy person has confined himself to worshipping desire, so there is no righteousness or guidance for him, and others may worship desire besides him. And if it were said: "He has taken his desire as his god," the meaning would be that he has confined his desire to the god, so he has no error, because his desire follows the command of the god, and others may share with him in worshipping the god. Abu Hayyan said: The meaning is that he has not taken a god except his desire, end of quote.

If it were reversed and said: "He has not taken a desire except his god," then when he does that he has stripped himself of desire, so he does not act upon it except in what agrees with the command of his god. And what clarifies for you the reversal of meaning through the change of order is that if you said: "So-and-so has taken his slave as his father," its meaning would be that he has magnified the slave; but if it were said: "He has taken his father as his slave," its meaning would be that he has humiliated the father. It makes no difference whether you present it in this way, in the pattern of the Qur'an, or you make one of them indefinite; you will not find your sense of it differing in that when one places the lowly first it ennobles it, and when one places the noble first it belittles it. Likewise if you said: "He has taken his stable as a mosque," or "his friend as a father," or reversed them. Had the fronting been merely for emphasis without difference in signification, He would have fronted desire in al-Jathiyah, since the context and the preceding passage concern it. The essential meaning is that the attribute of the deity has been obliterated and nothing remains but desire; so if desire were fronted, the meaning would be that the attribute of the deity has vanished and desire has overwhelmed him, and he looks to nothing but it, and recognizes no rule but it, as with clay in relation to pottery, equally. And Allah knows best.

Since none can turn away desire except Allah, there follows from his intense eagerness for their guidance the statement: ﴿Would you then be a guardian over him?﴾ And since his (ﷺ) intention was, out of eagerness for them and mercy towards them, to turn them back from error without fail, He expressed with the particle of elevation in His saying ﴿a guardian over him﴾, that is, on behalf of Allah, in a manner that would oblige you to turn him from his desire to what Allah has commanded by compulsion. You are not a guardian, but you are (ﷺ) a messenger; there is upon you only the conveyance, so do not let your soul go to waste over them in regrets.

Al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 25, verse 44:

When the turning away from desire was negated by compulsion through the matter of being a guardian (wikalah), He negated the turning away by willing choice through disparaging misguidance. So He mentioned the barrier to it in His saying, balancing what came before it, denying his reckoning (ḥusbān), not his being the reckoner (ḥāsib); or He denied that he is the reckoner, together with the sound intellect and firm judgment he possesses. The word ﴿taḥsabu﴾ (do you think) is coordinated with "takūnu" (you would be): ﴿Or do you think that most of them hear﴾, that is, these who were called, ﴿or understand﴾, that is, the hearing of one who is restrained even if he is not rational, like the beasts, ﴿or reason﴾ about what they see, even if they had no hearing, so that one might hope for their return by their own choice without compulsion.

Since this interrogative implies negation, He affirmed what it implied with His saying: ﴿Not even﴾, that is, they are not, ﴿but like cattle﴾, that is, in lacking reason, since they do not benefit from it, ﴿nay, they are further astray﴾, that is, than them, ﴿in the way﴾, because they are not restrained by what they hear while the cattle are restrained, and they do not give thanks to the benefactor who is their guardian, nor do they keep away from the wrongdoer who is their enemy, nor do they desire reward, nor do they fear punishment. That is because We have veiled the suns of their intellects with the shadows of the lofty mountains of their misguidance. Had they believed, those veils would have dispersed, and the lights of faith would have shone, so they would have perceived the wondrous meanings, and the hidden secrets would have become manifest to them.

﴿Indeed those who believe and do righteous deeds (p-396) — their Lord guides them by their faith﴾ [Yunus: 9]. Just as a person, though he may have sight, does not distinguish between sensible things unless the light of the sun shines upon them, so too a person, though he be rational and possessed of insight, his insight does not perceive the known meanings as they truly are unless the light of faith shines upon them, because insight is the eye of the spirit just as sight is the eye of the body. And since it is known that they hear and understand, and that what is negated is only their benefiting from that, it was a matter of wonder that they are turned away from it. So He, glory be to Him, followed this with His management of sensible matters as an example of spiritual matters, and because His action within the inner self illumines it, when He wills, with the sun of knowledge, just as His action in the outer self does, equally, as evidence of their being deprived of the benefit of what He has given them.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 25, verse 45:

When he (Allah) had made clear the obstinacy of those who raised objections against the proofs of the Maker, and the extremity of their ignorance and the corruption of their way, and since what is intended of the servant in recognizing that is that he should look at the acts of his Master with the eye of reality, a look by which other things vanish from him, so that he sees none but the Doer who chooses, He addressed the chief of the sincere who look in this way, urging the people of His love to the like of that. So He said, mentioning kinds of proofs that indicate the existence of the Maker, the comprehensiveness of His knowledge, and the all-encompassing reach of His power, pointing out that the one who looks at this proof, because of its clarity in indicating the Creator, is like one who looks upon the Creator, expressing it with the attribute of Ihsan (beneficence) to make him eager for continued contemplation of Him and turning toward Him: ﴿Have you not seen﴾. He indicated the greatness of the station and the loftiness of the rank by the particle of ultimate end ﴿to﴾ together with the one nearest of creation in rank and highest in station, and said: ﴿your Lord﴾, that is, the One who does good to you. The original would be "to His act." He indicated increased wonder at His affair by placing it in the form of a question, and said: ﴿how He extended the shadow﴾. The shadow is the darkness that prevents the meeting of the light of the sun. Abu 'Ubayd said: the shadow (zill) is what the sun removes, and that is in the morning, while the fay' (afternoon shade) is what replaces the sun, and that is after the zenith. Here the zill means the night, because it is the shadow of the earth, extended over about half of its surface for a period that screens the light of the sun by what faces its disk from the earth, until its spread stretched out and its tent was pitched, just as the shadow of their misguidance veiled the lights of their intellects, and the heedlessness of their natures prevented the penetration of their hearing. ﴿And had He willed, He would have made it stationary﴾, that is, the shadow stationary by perpetuating the night, which the sun does not remove, as in Paradise, according to His saying ﴿and extended shade﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 30], although there is a difference between them. But He did not will that; rather He made it moving by the sun's driving of it.

Since the bringing of the day after its non-existence, and the manifestation of the shadow by it after its obscurity, is a great matter, even though it has become trivial through much familiarity, He indicated it with the particle of delay and the station of majesty, and said: ﴿Then We made the sun over it a guide﴾, that is, by Our majesty, ﴿a guide﴾ that moves along with it wherever it moves. For were it not for the sun, it would not have become apparent that anything has a shadow, and were it not for the light (p-398) the darkness would not be known, and things are known by their opposites.

When its removal happened little by little after a period of time, it was likewise of great magnitude. He said, drawing attention to the excellence of what follows "thumma" (then) and its sequence ascending in the degrees of excellence: what is mentioned here is more excellent than what precedes it, and what precedes it is more majestic than what came before it. This likens the distance between the three stations in excellence to the distance between the events in time: ﴿Then We withdrew it﴾, meaning the shade. "Al-qabd" (withdrawal) is the gathering of what was spread out. ﴿To Us﴾, meaning toward the direction We intend, so that no one other than Us can turn it toward any other direction. Al-Razi, may Allah have mercy on him, said in al-Lawami': this attribution (to Us) is because the extreme shortening of the shade occurs at the extreme elevation of the sun, and height is the place of the angels and the direction of the heaven in which the provisions of the servants are, from which the rain and the relief descend, and toward which the hands of those who desire are raised and the eyes of those who fear are fixed. End of quotation.

﴿A gradual withdrawal﴾, meaning: it is, despite its being so small that its perception is difficult to achieve fully, easy for Us. We did not cease to reduce it little by little until it entirely vanished, or [left] only a little. Then We extended it again through the movement of the sun and its being screened by the surface of the earth, little by little, gradually, first by mountains, buildings and trees, then by hills, mounds and small hills and what is below those, until it was complete as it had been. In such a measured arrangement there are benefits beyond counting; had it been withdrawn, most of people's benefits from both shade and sunlight would have been lost together. The summary is that He makes their inner selves dark by screening them from the lights of knowledge, so they become like one walking in darkness, and their conduct in worldly affairs is like one walking at night on roads he has learned and trodden through repetition. The hadith of Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, concerning the soul that passed in the commentary on ﴿And good things are for good men﴾ [al-Nur: 26] is a sensory witness to this spiritual matter. And Allah is the Granter of success.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 25, verse 47:

When this verse included the night and the day, he (God) mentioned both explicitly as a proof of the truth and as a manifestation of the blessing upon creation: ﴿And He is the One who⦆ — that is, your Lord alone — ﴿who made⦆. Since what preceded concerning the shade was a subtle matter, He singled out its people with it; but since the matter of the night and the day is apparent to everyone, He generalized, saying: ﴿for you the night⦆ — that is, the one through which the extension of the shade is completed — ﴿as a garment⦆, that is, a covering that veils things from sight just as a garment covers; ﴿and sleep as rest⦆, that is, sleep, stillness and repose. It is an expression for it being a lesser death, suspending what was of perception, cutting off what was of awareness and movement, a sign for people of insight of death. Al-Baghawi and others said: the root of sabt (rest) is cutting off.

In His, glorified be He, making it so there are benefits, religious and worldly, that cannot be counted. Likewise His saying: ﴿and made the day a resurrection⦆, that is (p-400) life, movement and activity, by what He brought into being in it of wakefulness that reminds of the resurrection and prepares for movement, by returning what sleep had annihilated of all the senses. It is related that Luqman said to his son: "Just as you sleep and are awakened, so you die and are raised." Thus the verse is of ihtibak (the figure of omission by mutual reference): mentioning rest first as a proof of movement second, and resurrection second as a proof of folding and stillness first.

When He demonstrated His greatness through His disposal of meanings by bringing into existence and annihilating, and concluded that with death and life through near causes, He followed it with His disposal of concrete things in a similar manner, indicating death and life through distant causes. He began with what is near, because of its subtlety relative to meanings. In it is the *nashr* (an arrangement in which the items are listed in the same order as the earlier items they correspond to), with which he concluded what came before. So He said: ﴿And He is the One who sends the winds﴾, that is, He alone. The reading of Ibn Kathir in the singular is intended to denote the genus. The reading of the others in the plural is more indicative of choice, since the winds are sometimes a *ṣabā* (east wind) and sometimes a *dabūr* (west wind), sometimes a *shimāl* (north wind) and at another time a *janūb* (south wind), and other than that. ﴿as heralds﴾, that is, they stir up the clouds with their breezes, just as the spirits of bodies are dispersed by day. ﴿before His mercy﴾, for His servants, with rain.

Since the cloud is close to the wind in subtlety, and water is close to both of them and is a consequence of the clouds that the wind carries, He followed them with it. And since in His sending it down there is an indication of greatness, through His bringing it into existence there, holding it, and then sending it down at the intended time and in the chosen place according to need, which is not hidden, He changed the style, manifesting greatness, and said: ﴿And We send down from the sky﴾, that is, where none holds the water except Him, glory be to Him, ﴿water﴾. Then He substituted for it, to explain the blessing in it, saying: ﴿pure﴾, that is, pure in itself and purifying for others. It is a noun of instrument, like *saḥūr* (the pre-dawn meal) and *sanūn* (a toothstick), for that with which one eats the pre-dawn meal and cleans the teeth. Abu Hayyan transmitted from Sibawayh that it is a verbal noun of *taṭahhara* (the doubled form), applied in a way contrary to its verb. As for making it an intensive form of *ṭāhir* (pure), this yields no meaning beyond its being perfectly pure in itself, because its verb is intransitive.

Al-Biqa'i, *Nazm al-Durar*, on Surah 25, verse 49:

Since these acts indicate the resurrection but in a somewhat hidden way, He followed them with the fruit of this act as a clear proof of that. So He said, using the word "revive" for this purpose, and giving as the reason for the purity intended (*tahur*) the distance from everything that would defile it, such as saltiness, bitterness, sulphurousness, or the like, which would prevent the full benefit from it: ﴿That We may revive thereby﴾, i.e., by the water.

Since the intended purpose of reviving the earth with vegetation is the reviving of the lands in order to revive their people, He said: ﴿a dead land﴾. Even if it were salty, bitter, or sulphurous, there would be no power of reviving in it. And since He disliked that it should be understood as restricted to lands (*bilad*), the description was applied according to the place (p-402) so that it would encompass every place, and so He said: ﴿dead﴾, i.e., by what We bring forth in it of vegetation after it had become dry stubble and then dust, so that this would be a clear sign of Our power to resurrect the dead after they have become dust.

Since this is a context of majesty, through the manifestation of power, He added to it being a sign of the resurrection by the emergence of vegetation, which is a benefit for grazing, another great benefit in preserving [life] from death by drinking, just as the sign of revival preserves [life] by eating. So He said: ﴿and that We may give drink﴾, i.e., of the water. It is from *asqahu*, which is the augmented form of *saqahu*, and both are two dialects.

Ibn al-Qatta' said: "*saqaytuka sharaban wa-asqaytuka*" (I gave you a drink, and I gave you a drink), and Allah the Exalted gives drink to His servants and His land in the same way.

﴿of what We have created﴾, i.e., by Our majesty.

Since the blessing in sending down water is greater for livestock and the people of the desert and the like, because birds and wild beasts travel far in seeking [water] and so never lack what they drink, He specified them, saying: ﴿cattle﴾. He placed vegetation first because life of the cattle depends on it, and the cattle second because the full life of human beings depends on them. So when there is found what suffices them of giving drink, it [the water] is, in the easiest manner, sufficient. He followed this with His saying: ﴿and many people﴾, i.e., by Our preserving it in pools for the people of the desert who live far from rivers and springs, and others whom We wish. For He, the Exalted, does not give drink to all people equally, but He sends the rain upon whom He wills, turns it away from whom He wills, and gives drink to some people by other means. For this reason He made the mentioned things indefinite. This is as related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he said: "There is no year with more rain than another year, but Allah distributes that among His servants as He wills," and then he recited this verse.

Al-Baghawi said: Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Jurayj, and Muqatil mentioned it and traced it back to Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, as a marfu' report, [that he] said: "There is no year with more rain than another year, but Allah has distributed the provisions, placing them in the lowest heaven in this quantity, which descends each year in a known measure and a known weight. When a people commit sins, Allah diverts that [rain] to others, and when they all disobey, Allah the Exalted turns it away to the deserts and the seas." End of quotation.

The secret in this is that it was incumbent upon them to purify their outward and inward selves, and to purify others, so that they would be suited to His state of being purifying (*al-tahuriyya*). But when they became defiled with filth, they caused it to be turned away from them.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 25, verse 50:

When He, glory be to Him, mentioned that among the fruits of sending down the Qur'an in stages (nujūman) is the revival of hearts, which are the spirits of spirits, and followed it with what suits it, until He concluded with what He made a cause of life for bodies, this became a place for expecting a return to what is the life of spirits. (p-٤٠٤) He said, joining it to the subject of ﴿So that We may strengthen﴾ [al-Furqan: 32], drawing attention to another benefit of its being sent down in stages: ﴿And We have certainly diversified it﴾, i.e., We directed the Qur'an.

As Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) said, this is the intended meaning here, and what follows supports it. It means: in various modes of explanation, and We varied its ways in a manner that exhausts the eloquent, with very many meanings. ﴿Among them﴾, in every region, among every people, ﴿that they may take heed﴾ through the audible verses, with what We have fixed in their natural dispositions of rational proofs, and what is confirmed by the visible signs, even at the least degree of remembrance that would save them. This is what the idgham (assimilation of consonants, a rule of recitation) indicates.

Since the Qur'an necessarily leads to faith for anyone who is fair, it shows that whoever turns away from it is only stubborn, by His saying: ﴿But most people refused﴾, i.e., they did not want to, ﴿except disbelief﴾. Kufūran (كُفُورًا) is the verbal noun (masdar) of kafara, used with emphasis.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 25, verse 51:

When their obstinacy took the form of demanding that an angel be sent down to him so that he might be a warner together with him, this may have stirred in the soul a desire to grant their demand out of eagerness for their guidance. Therefore He first pointed out that there is no benefit in that, since the support that Harun (Aaron) gave Musa (Moses), peace be upon them both, did not avail the Copts anything. Second, He pointed out that the criterion for the obligation to believe a warner is the bringing of that which is unanswerable (i'jaz, inimitable proof), and this was present in the verses of the Qur'an, (p-405) which are variously expressed in every time and place with every kind of clarity, so that each verse of it stood in the place of a warner. He said, indicating that He had left that aside for wisdoms which He knows: ﴿And had We willed, We would have raised up in every town a warner﴾, i.e., by what We possess of greatness and the efficacy of Our word, ﴿in every town a warner﴾, i.e., from among mankind, or the angels, or others of Our servants, just as We apportioned the rain. For the dominion, as we mentioned at the beginning of the surah, is wholly Ours; We have no partner who would prevent that by what he possesses of right, nor a son who would prevent it by what he possesses of humility. But We did not do so, because of what the verses of the Qur'an contain of sufficiency in that regard, and because of what there is in your standing alone in the call of honour for you, and other wisdom besides.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 25, verse 52:

﴿So do not obey the disbelievers﴾ in what they intend of diverting you from calling upon it (the Qur'an), through the suggestions they put forward, or the flattery they display to you, or out of anxiety over the piercing warning, and they imagine that if you lessened it, they would hope to agree with you. ﴿And strive against them﴾, i.e., through the call, ﴿with it﴾, i.e., the Qur'an, which was previously mentioned in ﴿And We have indeed diversified it﴾ [al-Furqan: 50], by conveying its verses, whether they are bearers of good tidings or warners, and by arguing with its proofs, ﴿a great striving﴾, encompassing all outward and inward struggles, because in that there is the coming of many people to you and their gathering around you, so your affair is strengthened, your matter becomes great, ﴿their power weakens (p-406)﴾, and their fury is broken.

When he had mentioned the diversifying of the Criterion (al-Furqan) and its dispersal across all the lands, after stirring up the winds, spreading the clouds, and mixing water with earth to bring about the gathering and scattering of plants, He followed it, as a reminder of the blessing and a warning against incurring retribution, with the barrier between the kinds of water. There is no greater mixing than that of water, yet He gathered each kind separately and prevented it from mixing with the other, even though all of them mix with the earth, which is connected, one part to another. So He said, returning to the style of the third person (al-ghayba), as a reminder of the favour, by conjoining with the pronoun of "the Lord" in the verse of the shade:

﴿And He is the One﴾, that is, alone, ﴿who let the two seas flow freely﴾, that is, the two great and vast bodies of water, by making them agitated, as you observe in the nature of water. Al-Razi said: "He left them to themselves, as if He sent them forth in their courses, just as horses are sent forth into the pasture (al-marj). The root of marj indicates going and coming, agitation, and confusion."

Since agitation necessitates mixing, and the definite article (al) can be either for a specific reference (al-'ahd) or for a generic kind (al-jins), the listener is prompted to ask about this. It is answered that the intended meaning is the kind of water, sweet and salt, because al-bahr (sea) in origin means abundant water. It is also answered that He, glorified is He, prevented the two from mixing, even though the usual cause of mixing exists, by His overpowering power and His dominant majesty. So He said:

﴿This is sweet﴾, that is, sweet and palatable, ﴿fresh and pleasant﴾ (furat), that is, of extreme sweetness, reaching the utmost limit in it, to the point of being very sweet, with no difference between what is on the face of the earth and what is in its depths. ﴿And this is salty﴾, extremely salty, ﴿bitter﴾ (ujaj), that is, harsh and burning by its saltiness and bitterness, unfit for irrigation or drinking.

Perhaps by using the particle of proximity (hadha, "this") in both places He pointed to the existence of both places in close proximity, such that neither is confused with the other. Indeed, if one digs on the shore of the salt sea very close to it, the water that comes out is very sweet.

﴿And He placed﴾, that is, God, glorified is He, ﴿between them a barrier﴾, that is, a barrier of His power preventing them from mixing.

Since the two meet yet do not mix, each of them is in the position of one who transgresses against the other by mixing. So, glorified is He, completed the affirmation of the blessance in preventing their mixing with the phrase by which their custom is to seek refuge (at the time of seeking protection), likening each of them to one who seeks refuge, so that the statement, although it is a report, may bear the sense of seeking refuge. This is among the finest metaphors (isti'arat) and most evident of eloquence. So He said:

﴿And a forbidding barrier﴾, that is, a prevention, ﴿forbidden﴾, that is, prohibited from being accepted as lifted. All this emphasis indicates the grandeur of this verse, even though, through the intensity of familiarity with it, it has become, to the utmost degree, something people turn away from (p-408), so that by it His power may be known and His blessing may be thanked.

The commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 25, verse 54:

When the Exalted mentioned His power in keeping the water from mixing, He followed it with His power to mix it, lest it be thought that this was impossible. This affirms the act as a matter of choice and refutes the claim that it results from natures (*tabā'i'*, natural dispositions). So He said, referring to Himself by the pronoun as He had done before, to urge the mind to call to remembrance the acts and attributes mentioned earlier, so that the aspect (*ḥaythiyyah*) for which He repeated the pronoun may be known: ﴿And He it is who created from water a human being﴾, that is, He alone, by mixing it with clay, ﴿a human being﴾, as you witness Him bringing forth from it plants, trees, leaves and fruit. ﴿Then He made him﴾, that is, after that, through development through the stages of creation and the cycling through the phases of nurture, ﴿a lineage (*nasab*)﴾, that is, a male who is ascribed to him, ﴿and a marriage relation (*ṣihr*)﴾, that is, a female who is married, meaning one with whom he mixes. Thus He divided this water after its development into male and female, just as that water was made into two kinds, sweet and salty. He mixes the water of the male with the water of the female whenever He wills, and forms from it a human being, and He prevents that when He wills. Likewise, He distinguishes between the sweet and the salty, and mixes them together when He wills, by His all-encompassing knowledge and His perfect power. ﴿And your Lord is ever﴾, that is, the One who does good to you by sending you and sending down this Reminder to you, ﴿Powerful (*qadīran*)﴾ over everything, with the power He has shown in what He mentioned of originating these widely differing things from a single substance. (p-409) So He grants success to whomever He wills, making him sweet of taste and gentle of character, and He forsakes whomever He wills, making him bitter of character, greatly contentious, or of mixed character, deeply rooted in hypocrisy. So turn in supplication to this Lord, whose power encompasses all and whose knowledge is perfect.

When He had established for him, through these proofs, His power over everything, He said, expressing wonder at them, in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) relating to "your Lord" (rabbika). This returns to condemning their conduct in worshipping other than Him. He used the present tense (al-muḍāri') to indicate that if they did this once, it would be extremely strange, so how much more so when it is done as a constant and continuous practice? And to depict their state for added ugliness: ﴿and they worship﴾, i.e., the disbelievers, ﴿besides﴾, i.e., besides those whom they know to be lower in rank than ﴿Allah﴾, who possesses all the attributes of greatness, such that no harm or benefit comes except that it is in His hand.

Since this context is an enumeration of His favours, glorified is He, and since what moves a person to submission is hope for kindness or fear of humiliation, and since hope for kindness directs a person toward the Benefactor both in private and in public, He put benefit first and said: ﴿that which neither benefits them﴾, i.e., in any way.

Since fear only necessitates outward submission alone, He followed it with His saying: ﴿nor harms them﴾, i.e., at all, by removing any of Allah's blessings from them. (p-410) There is nothing more foolish in intellect than one who abandons the One in whose hand is every benefit and harm, while he is constantly surrounded by His blessings, in his wakefulness and his sleep, his yesterday and his today, and turns toward one who has no benefit or harm in his hand at all. He placed the explicit noun in the position of the pronoun to make clear the attribute that drives one to do what no sensible person would do, and He used the singular to belittle them, saying: ﴿and the disbeliever is﴾, despite his knowledge of its weakness and incapacity.

Since the disbeliever cannot be sincerely loyal to a believer as long as he remains a disbeliever, and his loyalty to others is present either actually or potentially, his hostility toward others is counted as nonexistence. Thus his hostility is specific to the friends of Allah, and this is more severe in condemning him. He indicated this by fronting the prepositional phrase, saying: ﴿against his Lord﴾, i.e., the One who bestows favour upon him and no other, ﴿as a helper﴾ (ẓahīran), assisting the satans of mankind and jinn against the friends of Allah. The use of "against" (ʿalā) indicates that, although he is in himself contemptible and insignificant, he is the agent of one who is high over something strong, harsh, and dominant over it, who assists against it, from the expression "the back of the earth" (ẓahr al-arḍ) for what is elevated and rugged from it, and "an affair that is apparent to you" (amr ẓāhir lak), i.e., dominant; and "the apparent" (al-ẓāhir) means strong and helping. This is because he assigns to the idols he worships a share of what Allah alone created, then he also assigns to them some of what he had named for Allah, and he opposes the friends of Allah among the prophets and others, sets up plots and wars against them, and harms them by word and deed, although he knows that Allah is with them, as he witnesses the breaking of customary patterns (khar' al-awāʾid) for them. So this is the act of one who regards nothing: ﴿Indeed they have become arrogant within themselves and have transgressed with a great transgression﴾ [al-Furqan: 21], and ﴿and do not exalt yourselves against Allah﴾ [al-Dukhan: 19]. In reality this is a mockery of the disbelievers, because they do what necessarily entails this consequence, which would never occur to any sensible mind.

Since the purpose of the passage is consolation for him (ﷺ), the implied sense is: "So hold fast to what We command you, and let not your concern at their rejection of what they are upon increase your distress, for We did not send you as a guardian over them." Upon this he (ﷺ) was followed by His saying: ﴿And We did not send you﴾, that is, with the greatness that is Ours.

Since the context of the surah is warning, because of what it mentions of their evil speech and the ugliness of their deeds, the expression regarding good tidings (bishara) was fitting with what indicates the abundance of the action and conveys the abundance of the one acted upon, as glad tidings of the abundance of the obedient; and regarding warning (indhar) with what requires that it be a constant attribute. So He said: ﴿only as a bringer of good tidings﴾, that is, to everyone who believes, ﴿and a warner﴾ to everyone who disobeys.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 25, verse 57:

When their answer to their saying ﴿Why has an angel not been sent down to him?﴾ [al-Furqan: 7] had come, and their saying ﴿or a treasure be thrown to him?﴾ [al-Furqan: 8] remained, attention was drawn to the greater importance of answering it by presenting it in the form of an answer, for one who might ask: "What should be said to them when they band together and attack the Message with what has preceded and with other things?" So He said: ﴿Say﴾, that is, to them, O most noble of creation in truth and most just of them in method, arguing against them by removing what could be a basis for accusation: (p-412) ﴿I ask of you no wage for it﴾, that is, for conveying the good news and the warning, ﴿any wage﴾, so that you might accuse me that I call you for its sake, or say: "Had a treasure been thrown to him, he would have been enriched by it and freed from this." It is as if he is saying: restraint from expanding in wealth is only disliked for one who begs people, and this was not one of my qualities before prophethood, so how much less after it? Then I have no aim at that time except your benefit. Then he emphasized this meaning by his saying, making an exception (istithna', exception, which is the criterion of generality): ﴿except whoever wills to take a way to his Lord﴾, that is, except the wage of whoever wills to take it, that is, who imposes on himself, opposes his desire, and makes for himself a way to his Lord. For when he is guided by the guidance of his Lord, he will have a reward like mine. I have no benefit from you except this. If you call this a wage, then it is what I seek. There is no doubt that it does not diminish anyone's share of his worldly life, so there is no harm to anyone in the worldly matter that is withheld from me. This conveys two benefits. The first is that he has no greed at all for anything that would diminish them. The second is the manifestation of utmost compassion, in that he regards their benefit, which leads them to their Lord, as a reward for himself.

When the aim was to turn them back from their obstinacy, and that was in extreme difficulty, and this speech would not repel their obstinate ones, who are the majority and whose harm is feared, (p-413) He joined to "Say" His words: ﴿And put your trust﴾, that is, show helplessness and weakness, submit, and rely in all your affairs, especially in confronting them with warning and in turning them back from their obstinacy.

Since the one entrusted (wakil) bears on behalf of the one who entrusts him the burden of what he has shown his inability to handle, and takes up its weights, until he becomes like one who carries for another a tangible thing, so that nothing of it remains upon the latter at all, He expressed this by the particle of elevation as an illustration, saying: ﴿upon the Living﴾. Trust in Him is not valid except by adhering to His obedience and turning away from whatever else.

Since the living among creatures die, He made clear that His life is not like the life of others, and so He said: ﴿Who does not die﴾, that is, there is no loss at all for one who trusts in Him, rather He is the one who takes charge of his interests in his life and after his death. Do not turn to anything else in any way, for it is perishing. ﴿And glorify Him with His praise﴾, that is, declare Him far above every deficiency, affirming for Him every perfection.

Since the one being consoled might occur to his thought that the one who consoles him is either unable to help him, or unaware of his opponent's sins, and since the context was a complaint about the turning away of those who convey the Qur'an and the harm that follows from it, He indicated by conjoining to something unmentioned that the implied meaning is: "Then He is sufficient as a helper for you." He joined to it (p-414) ﴿and sufficient﴾, specified the agent and confirmed it by introducing the preposition before it, saying: ﴿with Him regarding the sins of His servants﴾, that is, and all others besides them are His servants, ﴿as Knower﴾, nothing of them is hidden from Him, however fine it may be.

Then He described Himself with what implies that, together with His great power in dominion and origination, He is characterized by forbearance, comprehensive knowledge, and excellent management, so that the one who relies on Him may take Him as a model. So He said: ﴿Who created the heavens and the earth﴾, that is, despite their greatness, ﴿and what is between them﴾, of the expanse, the elements, the servants and their deeds, including sins and other things.

As for His saying ﴿Does not He who created know?﴾ [al-Mulk: 14], and His saying ﴿in six days﴾, it is a marvel for the ignorant fool and a training for the discerning scholar in forbearance, patience, and perseverance toward God's servants in calling them to God, and a reminder of His great power and of the comprehensive knowledge that it entails. The intended meaning is the measure of six of our days, for days only came into being after the creation of the sun. Affirming that the specification of this number is for a great wisdom, and likewise all His acts, even though we do not perceive that, is faith. God made Friday a festival for the Muslims because creation was gathered in it through the creation of Adam, peace be upon him, in its last hour.

Since the management of this dominion is a striking matter, He indicated it with the particle of delay, so He said: ﴿Then He established Himself on the Throne﴾, that is, He began to manage this dominion (p-415) which He originated and brought into being, and they and their sins are part of it, just as kings do in their realms. He is never heedless of anything at all, and no atom of essence or attribute comes into being except by a new creation from Him, glorified is He, refuting those among the Jews and others who say that this occurs only by the causes He arranged in eternity, and that He now has no act.

Since the one who is disobeyed, when he knows of the disobedience of one who disobeys him while he is able over him, does not give him respite, He indicated that He is otherwise, urging gentleness, by His saying: ﴿the All-Merciful﴾, that is, the One whose mercy preceded His wrath, who does good to the one who disbelieves in Him, let alone others. Therefore the most worthy of His servants to adopt this character are His messengers. The summary is that He originated this universe and began its management with the generality of mercy, in His kindness toward the one who hears Him reviling Him by ascribing to Him a son, and denying that He will restore him as He began him, while He, glorified is He, is able to take vengeance upon him, unlike the kings of the world, who do not show mercy to those who disobey them while they are powerless.

Since knowledge is necessarily tied to dominion, He made the following statement a consequence of that, in the manner of abstraction: ﴿So ask about Him﴾, that is, by means of your asking Him ﴿an expert (khabiran)﴾ (p-416) concerning these matters and every matter you desire, so that He may inform you of the reality of the affair in its beginning, its present state, and its outcome. Therefore let not your breast be constricted because of these called ones, for He sent you to them only while knowing them, and He will raise your standing over them and make the outcome good for you.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 25, verse 60:

When He had mentioned His beneficence toward them and His bounty upon them, He mentioned what they displayed of their disbelief in a place of gratitude, saying: ﴿And when it is said to them﴾, that is, to these people who move about in His blessings and are nourished by His grace and generosity, by whatever speaker it may be: ﴿Prostrate yourselves﴾, that is, humble yourselves through prayer and other acts, ﴿to the Most Merciful﴾, who is the source of every blessing you have, ﴿they say﴾, in the manner of the haughty and arrogant speech already explained in the meaning of ﴿supporter﴾ [al-Furqan: 55], ﴿And what is the Most Merciful?﴾, feigning ignorance of His knowledge, let alone ingratitude for His blessing, and referring to Him with the particle used for non-rational beings. Ibn al-'Arabi said: they used that expression either to indicate their ignorance of the attribute, not of the One described.

Then they marvelled at his command to this and objected to him, saying: ﴿Shall we prostrate ourselves to what you command us?﴾ So after feigning ignorance of His command and rejecting the one who calls to it, they again referred to Him with the particle used for non-rational beings. ﴿And it increases them﴾, this clear command which calls for turning towards and submitting, in gratitude for blessings and in hope of more, ﴿in aversion﴾, because of the satanic heat within them which drives them with a driving. There is no aversion equal to this aversion, nor is there any censure more eloquent than this.

When he had mentioned the state of the warner with whom the surah began, in his calling to the All-Merciful (al-Rahman), who, had nothing called to His worship but His mercy, it would have sufficed, so how much more with every beauty and majesty, and they denied him, the situation required that his affirmation be joined to the affirmation of what they know of the traces of His mercy. So he elaborated what had been stated in summary after mentioning the state of the warner, then of the King, prefacing it with the description of the Truth, which he made the opening of the surah, refuting what their denial contained of negating Him. He said: ﴿Blessed is He﴾, meaning He is established in a permanence that has no equal, ﴿who has placed in the sky﴾, which He had earlier stated He created, ﴿constellations﴾, and they are twelve constellations. They are for the wandering planets like dwellings for their inhabitants. They were named thus because of their visibility. He built upon them the affair of the earth, arranging its seasons by them and firmly establishing by them the livelihoods of its people.

Since the constellations, as is known, are not fit except by light, he mentioned it by the term "lamp" (siraj), saying: ﴿and placed in them﴾, meaning in the constellations, ﴿a lamp﴾, meaning a sun. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i (ʿAsim's reading transmitted by Hamzah and al-Kisa'i) read it in the plural form, to draw attention to its greatness in this respect, such that it is greater than thousands upon thousands of lamps. Thus the plural stands in place of a description, as He said of what follows: ﴿and a moon giving light﴾. He perfected the arrangement, by their movement within them and by other of their states, meaning that the knowledge of His necessary existence is beyond doubt, so how could any intelligent person doubt His existence or His mercy in this great, precisely made world, in which the affair of mercy is manifest?

When he had mentioned the two signs, he mentioned what they are signs of, saying: ﴿And it is He who made the night﴾, that is, the one whose sign is the moon, ﴿and the day﴾, whose sign is the sun, ﴿in succession (khilfah)﴾, that is, possessing a well-known state of alternation, so that this one comes after that one, in the opposite of its attributes, and takes its place in many of the things that are intended and the things that are decreed. Whoever misses something of one of them makes it up in the other. Ibn Jarir said: the Arabs say, "This one came after that one in succession (khilfah)," when something comes in place of something that has gone before it.

In al-Qamus it is stated that khalf and khilfah (with a kasrah) mean "that which alternates." On this reading the meaning is: He made them alternate in light and darkness, heat and cold, and other rulings. al-Razi said in al-Lawami': it is said, "The matter among them is in succession (khilfah)," meaning in turns, each one succeeding his companion; and "the people are khilfah," meaning they alternate.

Since the one who does not benefit from a thing is like one who lacks that thing, He restricted the making to the one who gathers its fruit, saying: ﴿for whoever wishes to remember﴾, that is, for whom remembrance is achieved, even at the lowest level. This is indicated by the idgham (assimilation of the two consonants, i.e., their merging into one doubled letter) in the reading of the majority, with the dhal and the kaf both pronounced with shaddah (doubled), in accordance with what his intellect indicates: that a change of such a magnificent form cannot occur without a changer who is capable, of immense power, and acting by choice. His remembrance thus leads him to faith, if he was an unbeliever. The reading of Hamzah with the lightening of the dhal (yadhdhakkara, from dhikr, "remembrance," without doubling) points to the fact that what the two signs indicate, namely the perfection of power and the all-encompassing knowledge which definitively proves the Oneness of God, is so manifest that it requires no reflection, but is achieved with the slightest attention. ﴿Or wishes to be grateful (shukur)﴾, that is, to give abundant and great thanks for the blessings of God, so that his wish moves him to gratitude if he is a believer, because of what his Lord has bestowed by bringing each of the two after the other has departed, so that he may gather their fruits. Had He made one of them permanent, the interests of the Hereafter would have been lost, weariness and boredom with it would have set in, there would have been negligence in matters that are fixed by times, laziness, and a slackening of resolve, which only the entry of another time stirs up to make up for them, and other matters which the Exalted, the Great, has perfected.

When He mentioned His servants whom He forsook by giving Satan power over them, so that they became Satan's party, He did not attribute them to any of His names. This signals their humiliation in His sight because of their own desires. These are the ones whom His saying at the beginning of the surah, ﴿a warner﴾ [al-Furqan: 1], explicitly refers to. He concluded with remembrance and thankfulness, alluding to His servants whom He purified exclusively for Himself. He had alluded to them earlier by specifying the description "al-Furqan" (the Criterion), so He followed that with mention of them. Conjoining with the whole statement in His saying ﴿And when it is said to them﴾ [al-Furqan: 60], He nevertheless raised them by beginning the sentence with them, as an honour: ﴿And the servants﴾.
