It is also permissible to say, and this is perhaps better, that when He described the disbelievers in this surah with what He described them with, of harshness and severity toward the Prophet (ﷺ), their enmity toward him, their backing against their Creator, and similar coarseness, and He concluded with remembrance and thankfulness, the implied sense was: "So the servants of Satan do not remember and do not give thanks, because of the hardness that is in them." He then conjoined their opposites to this implied statement, describing them with the opposites of their attributes and giving them the good news of the opposite of their recompense. So He said: And the servants of ﴿the Most Merciful﴾. He attributed them to Him as an elevation for them, although all creatures are His servants. He attributed them to the name denoting the most intense mercy, which those people denied, as good news for them. Then He described them with the opposite of what He described the arrogant who refuse to prostrate with, indicating that they had acquired, through this attribute to which they were attributed, a great matter. So He said: ﴿who walk﴾ and said: ﴿upon the earth﴾, as a reminder of what they are made of and what they will return to, and as an exhortation to strive for noble character in order to rise above it. He expressed their state by a verbal noun (masdar) for emphasis in their being characterized by its meaning, to the point that they became it. So He said: ﴿humbly﴾, meaning possessors of humility, that is, gentleness, kindness, calm, dignity, lowliness and modesty, neither harming anyone nor boasting, out of mercy toward themselves and others, not following what they were in of Satanic heat, and thus they were free of the shares of Satan, because whoever is from the earth and will return to it is fit for nothing but that. It is better to make this the predicate of "the servants," and that ﴿those will be rewarded with the lofty chamber﴾ [al-Furqan: 75] be a new, resumptive statement, anticipated as the conclusion is anticipated by one who infers.

When He mentioned what knowledge produced in them of action, He followed it with what forbearance produced of speech toward others. So He said: ﴿And when﴾, without "in" (in), because the attendance of its complement is customary, and He did not say "and those who," as in the other conjoined clauses, because the two qualities are like one thing in that both return to humility. ﴿The ignorant address them﴾, with some address, whether with ignorance or otherwise, at some time, that is, those who act contrary to knowledge and wisdom. ﴿They say: "Peace"﴾, meaning that which contains safety from every evil. The intended sense is not a greeting. Sibawayh transmitted this from Abu al-Khattab, saying: "Because the verse is, as is claimed, Meccan, and the Muslims were not then commanded to greet the polytheists. Rather it is, according to your view, a salutation of disengagement: there is no good between us and you, nor evil." End of quotation.

There is therefore no need to claim its abrogation (naskh) by the verse of fighting or by anything else, because overlooking the foolish and abandoning retaliation is praiseworthy in good manners, chivalry and the Law, and is safer for one's honour and piety. It seems that He stated the address without qualification, to inform that most of the speech of the ignorant is ignorance.

When he mentioned what passes between them and the creation, in speech and in action, and the usual case of that is that it is done openly by day, he mentioned what passes between them and their Creator of that kind in private by night. He stated these qualities as conjoined items with *wa* (and), to alert the reader that each one stands on its own in purpose, because of its great importance and its far-reaching effect. So he said: ﴿And those who spend the night﴾. *Al-baytutah* (spending the night) means that night overtakes you, whether you sleep or do not sleep. It is the opposite of *al-zulul* (resting in the shade by day). By placing ﴿for their Lord﴾ first, he conveyed exclusivity, meaning the One who is good to them through His compassionate mercy. They revive the night out of mercy for their own souls and in gratitude for His bounty.

Since prostration is the most emphatic of the pillars of prayer in drawing near to God, because it is the utmost form of humility, and because it is what the ignorant refuse, he placed it first for this reason. And it is known from the very beginning that standing in prayer [...]. So he said: ﴿prostrating﴾, and he followed it with what comes after it in hardship, to confirm that prostration is in its true form, so that both acts are purified for prayer. So he said: ﴿and standing﴾, meaning that they did not do the act of the ignorant, who are arrogant about prostration. Rather, as al-Hasan, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "Their day was in humility, and their night was in submission."

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 25, verse 65:

When he had mentioned their refinement of themselves for the creation and the Creator, he indicated that there is no self-admiration among them; rather, they are fearful, and that what moves them to this is faith in the Hereafter, which the ignorant have denied (p-423) ﴿They give what they give, while their hearts are fearful that they will return to their Lord﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 60]. They put forward the supplication for deliverance, out of concern for warding off harm and as an indication that they deserve it, even if they strive, because of their shortcoming in being unable to measure Him, glorified is He, with His true measure. So He said: ﴿And those who say, "Our Lord"﴾ meaning, O You who are good to us, ﴿turn away from us the punishment of Hell﴾ which has encompassed us because of our deserving it, unless Your pardon and mercy overtake us, by Your enabling us to meet whoever harms us with a cheerful countenance, not with a scowl. Then he gave the reason for their request by their saying: ﴿Indeed, its punishment was ever﴾ meaning, a state for which it was created, ﴿a continuous torment (gharam)﴾ meaning destruction and perdition that is persistent, encompassing whoever is attached to it, humiliating him, lasting for whoever is enticed by it, clinging to him and never separating from him, ﴿and we used to walk in the way of those who harmed us.﴾

When this attribute was established for it, it produced His saying: ﴿Indeed, it is evil as a place of settlement and residence﴾. That is, it (Hell) is at the utmost extreme in everything from which evil results, and it carries the meaning of "how evil" (bi'sat) in respect of all blameworthy qualities. ﴿A place of settlement﴾ means a place where one settles, and ﴿and residence﴾ means a place of lasting dwelling.

(p-٤٢٤) When he had mentioned their actions and sayings among themselves and toward creation, placing it first, and the Creator last, because their obligation comes after that, he mentioned their condition regarding their wealth. This was in view of the disbelievers' saying, ﴿Or a treasure be thrown down to him﴾ [al-Furqan: 8], and as guidance to the path of wealth, for whoever is moderate never falls into poverty. So he said: ﴿And those who, when they spend﴾, meaning upon creation or upon the Creator, whether in what is obligatory or in what is recommended, ﴿do not exceed the bounds﴾, meaning they do not go beyond the limit in expenditure through *tabdhir* (wasteful squandering, lit. "scattering"), so that they waste wealth in other than its proper due and thus become brothers of the devils, who are from the Fire, so that their conduct is the conduct of those devils. ﴿And do not withhold﴾, meaning they do not constrict, so that they neglect rights. Then he explained the just course by his saying: ﴿and it is﴾, meaning their expenditure is, ﴿between that﴾, meaning between the two extremes, that is, the conduct that must be kept far away.

When he knew that what lies between the two blameworthy extremes is justice, he stated it explicitly in his saying: ﴿a balance﴾, meaning justice, an equal midpoint between the two blameworthy traits, excess (*ifrat*) and deficiency (*tafrit*), taking on the quality of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if Allah were to expand provision for His servants, they would surely rebel in the earth; but He sends down in measure what He wills﴾ [al-Shura: 27]. This is the quality of the Companions of Muhammad (ﷺ), may Allah be pleased with them. They did not eat food for luxury and pleasure, nor wear clothing for beauty and adornment; rather they ate what satisfies hunger and aids in worship, and wore what covers the private parts and protects from heat and cold. (p-٤٢٥) ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "It is excessive (*sarf*) enough that a man should not desire anything without buying it and eating it."

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 25, verse 68:

When Allah mentioned the foundations of obedience with which they had adorned themselves, namely justice and kindness in deeds and words, with their bodies and their wealth, He followed this with what they had freed themselves from, namely the mothers of disobedience, which are indecency (al-fahsha') and evil (al-munkar). So He said: ﴿And those who do not invoke﴾, out of mercy toward their own souls and in order to put justice into practice, ﴿with Allah﴾, that is, the One who is singled out for the attributes of perfection, ﴿any other god﴾. The word "with" (ma'a), although it conveys that the other is distinct, [is used here because] when they were persistently obstinate, to the point that they would challenge by enumerating names, as was mentioned at the end of surah al-Isra' and surah al-Hijr, Allah the Exalted said, to cut off their obstinacy: ﴿another﴾, that is, invoking [Him] openly by worshipping Him, nor secretly through showing off (riya', ostentation in worship), lest they become like those upon whom the devils were sent, who incited them with an incitement.

Since He had not negated what necessitates the killing of their own souls through their ruin of them, He followed it with the killing of others, and said: ﴿nor kill﴾, that is, by what anger drives one to, ﴿the soul﴾, that is, out of mercy to creation and obedience to the Creator.

Since there are souls that have no sanctity, He clarified the intended meaning by His saying: ﴿which Allah has forbidden﴾, that is, its killing. That is, the Supreme King, to whom none is equal, has forbidden its killing with a great prohibition, ﴿except by right﴾, that is, by committing what makes its killing lawful.

When He mentioned open killing, He followed it with the hidden kind, the squandering of a child's lineage, and said: ﴿nor commit adultery﴾, that is, out of mercy toward the child that may come into being, to preserve its lineage, and out of mercy toward the woman who is violated and her relatives, that their sanctities not be violated, along with His mercy toward their own selves. Moreover, adultery also leads to killing and strife, and it involves causing a soul to come into existence wrongfully, just as killing causes that soul to be annihilated through that [same act]. It has been related in the Sahih, on the authority of ʿAbdullah ibn Masʿud (may Allah be pleased with him), that he asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Which sin is greatest (in one version: 'greatest') in the sight of Allah?" He said: "That you set up a rival to Allah while He created you." He said: "Then which?" He said: "That you kill your child for fear that it will share your food." He said: "Then which?" He said: "That you commit adultery with the wife of your neighbour." So Allah revealed, confirming that: ﴿And those who do not invoke with Allah any other god﴾ — the verse.

The confirmation of the verse by the report has been questioned, since the report speaks of a specific killing and a specific adultery, and of a qualification that it is "greatest," whereas the verse speaks of killing and adultery in general without any reference to their magnitude. There is no difficulty, because the verse does indicate the magnification of these acts in seven ways:

The first: the interposition between the mubtada' (المبتدأ, the subject), which is "and the servants of the Most Merciful" and what is conjoined to it, and the khabar (الخبر, the predicate), which is ﴿those will be recompensed﴾ [al-Furqan: 75], according to one of the two opinions, by mentioning the recompense of these three things specifically, and that indicates greater emphasis, which indicates magnification.

The second: the use of the demonstrative of distance (dhalika) in His saying ﴿And whoever does that﴾, that is, the act of great ugliness, despite the nearness of the things mentioned, which indicates that distance in rank.

The third: the expression "he will meet" (yalqa) together with the augmented verbal noun (masdar), which indicates an increase in meaning, in His saying ﴿he will meet a penalty (athaman)﴾, rather than "he will sin" (ya'tham), or "he will meet sin" (yalqa ithman), or "the recompense of his sin" (jaza' ithmihi).

The fourth: specification by multiplication, in his saying, as a new sentence: ﴿He will be multiplied﴾, that is, with the easiest matter, ﴿for him the punishment﴾, as recompense for his having followed his desires, with the satanic heat that is in them. This is according to the reading of Ibn 'Amir and Abu Bakr from 'Asim, with the nominative (*raf'*), and it is a *badal* (substitution, in grammatical apposition) for "يَلْقَ" (*yalqa*, "he will meet") in the reading of the majority (*al-jama'a*), because both lead to one meaning. The multiplication of the punishment, God knows best, is the bringing of part of it after part without interruption, just as he used to multiply his evil deed in the same way. The reading of Ibn Kathir, Abu Ja'far, Ibn 'Amir and Ya'qub with *tashdid* (the doubled form, "يُضَعَّفْ") conveys the general magnification of multiplication. The reading of the rest with *mufa'ala* ("يُضاعَفْ") requires it in relation to one who competes with another in it, so it is more eloquent.

The fifth: the striking of awe with his saying ﴿on the Day of Resurrection﴾, which is more terrifying than other times by an incomparable degree.

The sixth: the announcement of *khulud* (abiding), which is its first degree, namely that it is a long stay. So he said, conjoining it in both readings to "يُضاعَفْ": ﴿and he will abide in it﴾.

The seventh: the explicit statement with his saying ﴿humiliated﴾, and perhaps it is to exclude what is possible: that some of the disobedient of this community, whom God intends to punish, know that they will be saved and enter Paradise, so their staying, with knowledge of the outcome, is not in the manner of humiliation. When the matter became great from these aspects, it is known that each of these sins is grave. If the more general is grave, the more specific that is mentioned is greater than the absolute general, because it adds to it what made it specific. Thus it is established by this that they are major sins, and that killing a child and adultery with the neighbour's wife are greater for what has been mentioned. So the way in which the verse confirms the hadith is clear. Do not say: the demonstrative reference returns to the whole group, so the awe is specific to one who commits the whole group of these sins, because we say: the context refutes this, since the repetition of "لا" (*la*, "not") conveys, as al-Radi verified, that the negation applies to the occurrence of the three traits both together and separately. So the meaning is: they do not commit any of them. Thus "and whoever does that" meant "and whoever does any of that", so that the affirmation responds to what the negation applied to, and harmony is achieved. As for the verse not conflicting with the order, it is from two aspects. The first is that the basic principle in putting something first is attention to what the verse was addressed for, namely deterrence, which conveys severity, so each of them is higher than what follows it.

The second is that the *waw* (conjunction "and") does not contradict this, and the verbs were mentioned in an order just as they were ordered in the hadith with "ثُمَّ" (*thumma*, "then"), so it is intended that they indicate order. God is the Guide.

When God, glorified is He, had completed the warning to the wicked regarding these burdens of sin, He followed it with an encouragement for the righteous (p. 429) to turn to God, the Mighty, the Forgiving. So He said: ﴿Except for one who repents﴾, that is, returns to God from anything of these deficiencies that he had been engaged in, ﴿and believes﴾, that is, establishes the foundation without which no deed is sound, which is faith, or confirms its existence, ﴿and does righteous deeds﴾. Since turning back from it is more difficult, He emphasized it, saying: ﴿righteous deeds﴾, that is, founded upon the basis of faith. Then He increased the encouragement by using the particle "fa" (so), linking the reward to the condition, as a proof that the condition is its cause, and said: ﴿those﴾, that is, the exalted in station, ﴿God will replace﴾. He mentioned the Greatest Name to magnify the matter and to indicate that He, glorified is He, has no rival, ﴿their evil deeds with good deeds﴾, that is, because of their regret over those evil deeds, since they were not good deeds, so He records for them their reward through their sincere resolve to perform them had they faced their affairs differently than they had turned away from them. So when one of them sees his evil deeds replaced with good deeds, he wishes that his evil deeds had been even more numerous! It has been related that some of them say: "My Lord! I have evil deeds that I did not see," narrated by Muslim at the end of the Book of Faith in his Sahih, from Abu Dharr, may God be pleased with him, traced to the Prophet.

Since this is a matter for which no such custom had occurred, He informed that it is His attribute, exalted is He, eternally and forever. So He said, repeating the Greatest Name lest anything of what has passed restrict His forgiveness: ﴿And God was﴾, that is, the One who possesses majesty and honor, with regard to His knowledge, ﴿Forgiving﴾ (p. 430), that is, Concealing of the sins of everyone who repents on this condition, ﴿Merciful﴾ toward him, by treating him with honor as one treats one who is shown mercy, so He gives him a good deed in place of every evil deed. Al-Bukhari related from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, that this verse was revealed concerning the people of polytheism. When its first part was revealed, the people of Makkah said: "We have then made equals to God, killed the soul that God has forbidden, and committed the abominations." So God revealed ﴿except for one who repents﴾ — to — ﴿Merciful﴾.

It is also related from him that he said: "This is a Meccan verse, abrogated (naskh) by a Medinan verse, which is in Surat al-Nisa'," meaning on the assumption that it is general, covering the polytheist and others. It is also related from him that he said concerning the verse of al-Nisa': "It was revealed among the last of what was revealed, and nothing abrogated it."

The answer to this has already been given in Surat al-Nisa'. Likewise is what al-Bukhari related from him in the Tafsir (exegesis) section: "Some people from among the polytheists had killed and done much, and committed fornication and done much, so they came to Muhammad ﷺ and said: 'What you say and call to is indeed good, if only you would inform us that there is an expiation for what we have done.' So there was revealed: ﴿And those who do not invoke with God another deity, nor kill the soul which God has forbidden except by right, nor commit unlawful sexual intercourse﴾ [al-Furqan: 68], and there was revealed: ﴿O My servants who have transgressed against themselves, do not despair of the mercy of God﴾ [al-Zumar: 53]."

When the particle *fa'* (so/then) indicated causation (*al-tasbib*, the sense of consequence), and the emphasis of the verb by the verbal noun indicated the need for a great deal of work [p. 431], which may exceed human capacity, and [the verse] alluded to the path toward it through the two great attributes, it followed this with an explanation of the way to it by means of what God has made customary, saying: ﴿But whoever repents﴾, that is, turns away from disobedience, whether it be disbelief or less than that, ﴿and does righteous deeds﴾, confirming the truthfulness of his claim to repentance.

Since this is in the context of encouragement, He removed from it [the verb's] emphasis, saying: ﴿righteous﴾, even if each of his intention and his deed is weak. God, glorified be He, encouraged this with His saying, informing that he reaches God: ﴿then indeed he turns﴾, that is, returns, arriving ﴿to God﴾, that is, the One who possesses the attributes of perfection; so He accepts repentance from His servants and pardons misdeeds. ﴿A [sincere] return﴾, that is, a very great return, by God making him desire righteous deeds, so that every day he continues to grow in his intention and his deed. What was heavy upon him becomes light, what was difficult becomes easy for him, and what was hard becomes simple for him, as was previously mentioned in ﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds, their Lord guides them by their faith﴾ [Yunus: 9]. He continues thus until God loves him, so that He becomes his hearing with which he hears, his sight with which he sees, his hand with which he strikes, and his foot with which he walks, by enabling him to do good, so that he hears only what pleases Him, and so on. Whoever takes this according to its apparent meaning, upon him is the curse of God, for opposing the consensus (*ijma'*, scholarly agreement) of the Muslims.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 25, verse 72:

When He, glorified is He, described His servants as adorned with the foundations of virtues and purified of the mothers of vices (p-432), and as desiring repentance, because man, by his weakness, never ceases to fall short, and He had praised them, after the first of their attributes, for forbearance toward ignorance, He praised them before the other of their eulogies, and He followed their abstention from fornication by abstaining at the root from idle talk (al-lagh), which is the greatest of the preliminaries to fornication. So He said: ﴿And those who do not witness﴾, meaning they are not present, deviating with desire as the fire does, from which Satan comes, ﴿falsehood (al-zoor)﴾, meaning the speech that deviates from truth, whether it is a lie or close to one, let alone that they utter it and approve of it.

Ibn Jarir said: The root of zoor is to beautify a thing and describe it contrary to its real description, until it appears to the one who hears or sees it that it is other than what it is. It is thus the embellishing of falsehood with what gives the impression that it is truth. Shirk may enter into this, because it beautifies itself to its adherents until they think it is truth while it is falsehood. Singing (al-ghina') also enters into it, because it too is beautified by the trilling of the voice until the listener finds his hearing of it sweet. Lying also enters into it, through its doer's embellishment of it until he thinks it is true.

He then conjoined to it what is more general than it, saying: ﴿And when they pass by idle talk﴾, meaning that which ought to be cast aside and nullified, whether it is of the kind of lying or of pointless frivolity that profits nothing. Ibn Jarir said: In the speech of the Arabs it is every speech (p-433) or deed of falsehood that has no reality and no basis, or that which is considered ugly.

﴿They pass by with dignity (kiraman)﴾, meaning commanding the good and forbidding the evil, if a command or prohibition concerns them, by gesture or by word, according to what they judge beneficial; or turning away, if none of that is suitable, lest it stir up a greater corruption than that or the like, out of mercy toward themselves and others. As for their presence at such things and their silence, that is not permitted, because spectators of everything that the Sharia has not sanctioned are partners of its doers in sin, since their presence and their gazing are evidence of approval of it, and a cause of its existence and its increase.

When he had mentioned their attribute by which they excelled, he pointed to the attribute of the ignorant by which they sank low, saying: ﴿And those who, when they are reminded﴾ of the signs of their Lord, i.e., when others remind them, whoever they may be, because they recognize the truth by itself and not by the one who speaks it. ﴿of the signs of their Lord﴾, i.e., the One who enabled them to remember His favor toward them in His good upbringing of them, by taking heed of the signs that are seen and heard. ﴿do not fall﴾, i.e., they do not act like those who fall down upon them, the ones who feign deafness and blindness to them. Then he increased the explanation of their turning away and their hindering from them, saying, drawing attention to the fact that what is negated is the restriction and not the restricted, namely the falling down, but rather it exists and is not negated, with the attribute of hearing and sight: ﴿deaf and blind﴾, i.e., as the hypocrites and disbelievers do in turning toward them, hearing them and taking heed, and turning away from them as a concealing of what they knew of their truth and a veiling of what they saw of their light, the act of one who neither hears nor sees, as has preceded (p-434) concerning Abu Jahl, Abu Sufyan and al-Akhnas ibn Shariq. This is a description of the servants of the Most Merciful by performing the opposite of this, i.e., that they fall down when hearing them and weep over them, falling as a hearer who benefits from his hearing, a seer who benefits from his sight and insight, prostrating and weeping, as has preceded at the beginning of their attributes, even if they do not reach the highest degrees of insight, by what the intensification indicated by the addition of the nun to the plural of blindness (ʿumyān) points to.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 25, verse 74:

When he (Allah) mentioned this quality, which bears fruit for what follows the first sincere attribute (al-khalasah), he concluded with what produces the first attribute. So He said, indicating that leadership in religion should be sought and desired: ﴿And those who say﴾, knowing from them that, after their having attained all that has passed, they are worthy of leadership: ﴿Our Lord, grant us from our spouses﴾ those whom You have joined with us, as You did for Your Prophet ﷺ, when You praised his wife in Your eternal speech and made her praise recited over the succession of ages and years. ﴿And our offspring as a comfort to our eyes﴾. Since the God-fearing (al-muttaqun), those who perform obedience and rejoice in it, are few in comparison with the disobedient, he used the plural of paucity (jam' al-qillah) and made it indefinite, saying: ﴿eyes﴾, meaning: from among the deeds or from among the doers who will follow us, because the closest are the most deserving of what is good. Nothing delights the believer more, or comforts his eye more, than seeing his beloved obey Allah. Therefore they asked only that Allah be obeyed so that their eyes would be comforted. So "min" (from) is either like it in: "I saw from you a lion" (i.e., a partitive/explicative use), or it is in its own original sense, and the comfort is the deeds, meaning: grant us from them righteous deeds. So they made the deeds of those who are dear to them a gift to them. The root of qurrah (comfort) is coolness, because the Arabs are harmed by heat and find relief in coolness, so this was made a metaphor for joy. ﴿And make us﴾, meaning: ourselves and them, ﴿leaders for the God-fearing﴾, meaning: in general, from among relatives and strangers alike.

Since what is sought from the Muslims is unity in obedience, so that the word in following may be one, they indicated this by using the singular for "imam", even though the intended meaning is the category. So they said: ﴿imaman﴾ (as leaders), meaning: that we would be scholars who are humble and modest, as is the nature of the leadership of piety in conveying humility and tranquility, so that we may obtain the great reward, since a person has his own reward and the reward of whoever is guided by him and acts by his action. "Whoever establishes a good sunnah will have its reward and the reward of whoever acts by it until the Day of Resurrection," and the opposite of this.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 25, verse 75:

When He (glory be to Him) described His believing servants with the opposite of the attributes of the disbelievers, namely gentleness and tranquility, humility and forbearance, serenity, gratitude to their Lord, eagerness toward Him and awe of Him.

Al-Razi said: He described their walking, their speech, their standing before Him, their supplication, their spending, their chastity, their vigilance and wakefulness, their sincerity, their love and their sincere counsel. The listener, having come to know what the disbelievers receive, longs to know what awaits them with Him, so He began the report about it by magnifying their status, saying: ﴿Those﴾, that is, those of high rank and great station. Since the intended matter is the recompense, He used the passive form in His saying ﴿will be rewarded﴾, that is, by grace from Allah for what He enabled them to do of these pure deeds and pure states, ﴿the high chamber﴾, that is, the one which, by its loftiness, its vastness and its goodness, is not like any other chamber, for it is the furthest point of desire and the ultimate goal of aspiration; they seek no substitute for it and do not desire any exchange for it. It is every lofty, elevated building, and it is apparent that what is meant by it is the category (of chambers).

Since the abodes are in the utmost hardship due to their conflict with the desires and passions of the soul and the inclination of the body, He encouraged them toward it by making it the cause of this recompense, saying: ﴿for that they endured patiently﴾, that is, they exercised patience in the command of their Lord and in the bitterness of their strangeness among the ignorant, in their deeds, their words and their states, and in other meanings of their majesty.

Since a dwelling is not pleasant except with honor and safety, He said: ﴿And they will be met﴾, that is, Allah will make them encounter with the easiest matter. According to the reading of Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Abu Bakr from ʿAsim, with the lightened form and the active voice, the matter is clear. ﴿Therein they will be greeted with a salutation﴾, that is, a supplication for life from some of them to others, and from the angels, whose supplication is not rejected and whose report is not doubted, for they speak on behalf of Allah; and this is in the manner of honor and exaltation in place of what the servants of Satan humiliated them with. ﴿And peace﴾, that is, from Allah and from the angels and others, and safety from every calamity, in place of what those (disbelievers) inflicted upon them of afflictions.

Since this (verse) speaks explicitly of their continued life in safety, and implicitly of the great honour they receive, it indicates that they will not depart from it, by His saying: ﴿Abiding therein﴾, that is, in the chamber, in place of what they had been driven from their homes, until they emigrated. It also indicates the loftiness of its status and the greatness of its worth by displaying its praise in the form of wonderment, so He said: ﴿How good it is﴾, that is, how excellent it is, ﴿as a place of rest (mustaqarran)﴾, that is, a place of settling, ﴿and a place of dwelling (muqaman)﴾, that is, a place of residence.

When the matter of al-Rahmaniyya (the Most Merciful's all-encompassing mercy, the attribute of Ar-Rahman) was established, and the matter of the Most Merciful and the supplication His servants owe Him, which is submission and sincerity, became manifest, He concluded their good attributes with supplication, which is the true meaning of calling upon Him and indicates sincerity in submission. He mentioned the goodness of their recompense and the nobility of their final return. Then He commanded the Warner (the Prophet ﷺ) to say to the servants of Satan, who were arrogant toward prostrating to the Most Merciful and toward acknowledging and believing, so that they would turn back from disobedience and the believers would increase in obedience and faith: indeed, your Lord does not reckon anyone who does not call upon Him. Whoever abandons His supplication should await the lasting punishment. So He said: ﴿Say: "What would my Lord care for you..."﴾, that is, He would not reckon (you) or regard you (p-٤٣٨) or mind you, and would not make you among those who are counted for anything at present, taking "ma" as a negation. ﴿with you﴾, that is, O disbelievers. ﴿My Lord﴾, that is, the One who shows kindness to me and to you through His Most Merciful attribute, who singles me out for kindness through His Most Compassionate attribute. He specified (the pronoun) by the idafa (possessive construction) only because He acknowledged (Lordship) to the Prophet alone, not to them. ﴿were it not for your calling﴾, that is, your calling upon Him at the time of your hardships, to which you rush in submission to Him so that He may save you. When you do this, He rescues you from what you are in, dealing with you as one who minds a human being, reckons with him and regards him. And were it not for His calling you to worship Him, out of mercy toward you, so that you purify your souls and clear your deeds and do not become fuel for the Fire. ﴿Then you have denied﴾, that is, the result of your ill natures was the opposite of what was fitting for you of gratitude and good, in that you followed deliverance with denial, you confirmed and combined denial of the Most Merciful after His mercy toward you through clarification, despite your weakness and helplessness, you abandoned that calling upon Him, worshipped idols, and attributed to Him a son and other falsehoods. Or (the meaning is): He would not reckon you with any reckoning, were it not for your calling upon Him in times of hardship; so He reckons you for that purpose a certain kind of reckoning, namely the term He set for you in this world and nothing beyond it, because you have denied. Or: He would not do anything with you were it not for His calling you to obedience to Him, because you have denied and thus became worse than cattle; so He called you, and as a result of His calling you, you confronted the Caller with denial. The summary is that there is nothing in you now (p-٤٣٩) that is fit for Him to reckon you for except supplication, because you are deniers. I said "now" (al-an) only because "ma" (in this negative sense) enters only upon a present-tense verb with the meaning of the present, unlike "la." ﴿Then it will be﴾, that is, as a result of your denial He will requite you for it, yet with His might, power and free choice He does not hasten against you; rather ﴿it will be﴾ the recompense of this denial at the end of the terms He has set for you, and everything far away to you is near to Him, and everything that is coming is near; so prepare yourselves and reckon for that day. ﴿inseparable﴾, that is, a binding that will never be separated from you in any condition. This is an alert to their weakness, helplessness, humiliation and subjugation, since the thing bound cannot be otherwise. Thus at the Battle of Badr He took captive some of those who fit this threat. The end of the surah thus corresponds to its beginning with the warning of the Criterion (al-Furqan) to whoever denied the true reality of the Most Merciful. And Allah is the Granter of success in faith.
